fuentes/monedas-de-los-reyes-britanos/re.texto: From the mid-2nd century BC gold coins from Belgic Gaul reached Britain, and from the late 2nd century coins were minted on the island. Around 50 BC the first ones with names appear, such as COMMIOS, followed by those of Tasciovanus, Cunobelinus, Epillus, Verica, Adminius and the Iceni kings, with titles such as REX or RICON and place names such as CAMV (Camulodunum), VER (Verulamium) and CALLEV (Calleva); their motifs shift from horses and abstract heads to imitations of Roman coins.

fuentes/monedas-de-los-reyes-britanos/po.texto: They are almost the only written texts produced by the Britons themselves before the conquest, and they allow the reconstruction of dynasties that Roman sources barely mention. The Celtic Coin Index of Oxford records tens of thousands of pieces; the reading of the legends and the attribution to specific kings are largely hypothetical.

fuentes/inscripcion-del-arco-de-claudio/.texto: Inscription on the Arch of Claudius in Rome

Inscription from the triumphal arch that the Senate dedicated to Claudius in Rome in 51-52 for the conquest of Britain (CIL VI 920), preserved in fragments. It says that the emperor received the surrender of eleven kings of Britain “without any loss” and that he was the first to subject to the power of the Roman people the barbarian peoples beyond the Ocean.
It is the official Roman version of the conquest, from the same year in which Caratacus was displayed in Rome; the figure of eleven kings is the only one given by a document of the period.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-togidubno/resumen.texto: Dedicatory stone of a temple to Neptune and Minerva found in Chichester in 1723 (RIB 91), dedicated by a guild of smiths “with the authority of Tiberius Claudius [...]gidubnus,” according to the current reading “great king of Britain.” The names Tiberius Claudius indicate the citizenship received from Claudius. The stone is worn: the beginning of the name is lost, and the title was previously read as “king and legate of Augustus in Britain.”

fuentes/inscripcion-de-togidubno/por_que.texto: It confirms what Tacitus says about a client king loyal to Rome, and shows a British king using Roman titles and gods. The form Togidubnus is a restoration (Murgia, 1977): the manuscripts of Tacitus give both Cogidumnus and Togidumnus, and the stone supports the ending -dubnus without deciding the initial letter.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-togidubno/leer.0..texto: Text, translation and photo (RIB 91), Roman Inscriptions of Britain

fuentes/lapida-de-clasiciano/titulo.texto: Tombstone of the procurator Julius Classicianus

fuentes/lapida-de-clasiciano/resumen.texto: Funerary monument of the procurator Gaius Julius Alpinus Classicianus, fragments of which were found in London in 1852 and 1935 (RIB 12), set up by his wife, Julia Pacata, daughter of Julius Indus, a Treveran noble who had helped Rome in Gaul.

fuentes/lapida-de-clasiciano/por_que_imp.texto: It confirms the post of the procurator who, according to Tacitus, secured the replacement of Suetonius Paulinus after Boudica's revolt, and shows Romanized Gauls in the administration of Britain. It is in the British Museum.

fuentes/lapida-de-clasiciano/leer.0.titu.texto: Text, translation and photo (RIB 12), Roman Inscriptions of Britain

fuentes/tablillas-de-vindolanda/autor.texto: Soldiers, officers and families of the Vindolanda fort

fuentes/tablillas-de-vindolanda/resumen.texto: Hundreds of wooden tablets written in ink, found since 1973 at the Roman fort of Vindolanda: letters, lists of supplies, troop reports and a birthday invitation from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, the oldest known Latin text written by a woman. A military report says that the Britons do not wear body armor, that they have many cavalrymen, and that the “little Britons” (Brittunculi) do not ride to throw javelins.

fuentes/tablillas-de-vindolanda/por_que_.texto: They were the oldest handwritten documents from Britain until the discovery of the Bloomberg tablets in London (from 57), and they show the daily life of a garrison before Hadrian's Wall. The derogatory diminutive Brittunculi is one of the few testimonies of how soldiers spoke of the native people.

fuentes/tablillas-de-vindolanda/leer.0.t.texto: Corpus of the tablets with text and translation, Roman Inscriptions of Britain

fuentes/tablillas-de-bloomberg/soporte.texto: Wooden wax tablets, written with a stylus

fuentes/tablillas-de-bloomberg/resumen.texto: About four hundred wooden tablets found between 2010 and 2013 in the excavations of the Bloomberg building in the City of London, of which Roger Tomlin was able to read about ninety from the marks the stylus left in the wood (2016). They are letters, contracts, accounts and court documents from early Londinium; the oldest dated one is an acknowledgment of debt of 8 January 57, three or four years before the city was destroyed by Boudica.

fuentes/tablillas-de-bloomberg/por_que_i.texto: They are the oldest handwritten documents from Britain, and they show that Londinium was already, before the revolt, a center of trade and lending, the world that according to Cassius Dio angered the Britons; almost all the tablets remain illegible.

fuentes/tablillas-de-bloomberg/leer.0.ti.texto: Edition by Roger Tomlin with text, translation and photos, Roman Inscriptions of Britain

fuentes/historia-de-herodiano/titulo.texto: History of the Empire after Marcus

fuentes/historia-de-herodiano/resumen.texto: History in eight books of the emperors from the death of Marcus Aurelius (180) to 238. In Book III it tells of Septimius Severus's campaign in Britain: the northern Britons live in marshes, go almost naked, wear iron around the neck and waist as ornament, tattoo their bodies with animal figures, and do not wear armor so as not to cover those designs.

fuentes/historia-de-herodiano/por_que_im.texto: Together with Cassius Dio, it is the source for Severus's campaign; Herodian is imprecise and fond of rhetoric, and his description repeats commonplaces about barbarians, although the report of the tattoos coincides with the name “Picts.”

fuentes/historia-de-herodiano/leer.0.tit.texto: English translation by E. C. Echols (1961), Wikisource

fuentes/panegirico-de-constancio/resumen.texto: Speech of praise delivered in 297 before the caesar Constantius Chlorus, probably in Trier, for the recovery of Britain after the usurpation of Carausius and Allectus. Comparing the Britain of Caesar with that of his own time, it says that then the Britons were only used to enemies such as the Picts and the Hibernians (the Irish), “still half-naked”: the first known appearance of the name of the Picts (VIII.11).

fuentes/panegirico-de-constancio/por_que.texto: It is part of the collection of the Latin Panegyrics, official speeches by Gallic orators; it is court rhetoric, but it dates the name of the Picts. The well-known phrase “the Caledonians and other Picts” does not come from this speech but from the panegyric to Constantine of 310 (VI.7).

fuentes/panegirico-de-constancio/leer.0..texto: “XII Panegyrici Latini”, Baehrens edition (1874), Internet Archive

fuentes/historia-nueva-zosimo/resumen.texto: History of the Roman Empire written by a pagan official of Constantinople, who blames Christianity for the decline. In Book VI it tells that in 409 the Britons, abandoned by Constantine III, took up arms, expelled the Roman officials and governed themselves, and that Honorius wrote to “the cities of Britain” that they should defend themselves on their own.

fuentes/historia-nueva-zosimo/por_que_im.texto: It is the main source on the end of Roman rule in Britain; Zosimus copies Olympiodorus, a contemporary of the events, but some historians believe Honorius's letter was addressed to the Bruttii, in Italy.

fuentes/cronica-de-prospero/resumen.texto: Continuation of Jerome's chronicle written by a layman from Aquitaine who worked in Rome with Pope Leo I. For 429 it records the dispatch of Germanus of Auxerre to Britain against the Pelagians, and for 431 the ordination of Palladius as the first bishop “of the Scots who believe in Christ”; in another work, Contra Collatorem (against John Cassian, author of the Conferences), he praises Pope Celestine for having made “the barbarian island” Christian while keeping the Roman one Catholic.

fuentes/cronica-de-prospero/por_que_impo.texto: It is the only contemporary source on the beginning of Christianity in Ireland and one of the few on Britain in the 5th century.

fuentes/cronica-de-prospero/leer.0.titul.texto: Chronica minora I, Mommsen edition (MGH, 1892), Internet Archive

fuentes/vida-de-german-constancio/resume.texto: Life of the bishop Germanus of Auxerre written around 480 by the priest Constantius of Lyon. It narrates his two journeys to Britain against the Pelagians, the public debate, the visit to the tomb of Saint Alban and the “Alleluia victory” against Picts and Saxons, as well as his intercession for the Armoricans with the Roman government.

fuentes/vida-de-german-constancio/por_qu.texto: It is almost the only continental account of post-Roman Britain, written half a century later and with the aims of a hagiography, but it shows a society still organized in the Roman manner.

fuentes/cronica-galica-de-452/resumen.texto: Anonymous chronicle written in southern Gaul that runs down to 452. For 441 it records that “the Britains, until then punished by various disasters, pass under the power of the Saxons.”

fuentes/cronica-galica-de-452/por_que_im.texto: It is the closest report in time to Saxon rule in Britain and contradicts Bede's date (449); its chronology is imprecise and it is not known which part of the island it refers to.

fuentes/cronica-galica-de-452/leer.0.tit.texto: Chronica minora I, Mommsen edition (MGH, 1892), Internet Archive

fuentes/de-excidio-britanniae/resumen.texto: Latin sermon in three parts: a history of Britain from the Roman conquest (with errors, such as dating the walls to the end of the Empire), the arrival of the Saxons invited by a “proud tyrant,” the resistance of Ambrosius Aurelianus and the victory of Mount Badon; a condemnation of five British kings of his time (Constantine, Aurelius Conanus, Vortiporius, Cuneglasus and Maglocunus) and another of the clergy. Gildas presents the invasion as God's punishment for the sins of the Britons, in the manner of the biblical prophets.

fuentes/de-excidio-britanniae/por_que_im.texto: It is the only narrative source written by a Briton between the 5th and 6th centuries, and Bede and everything later depend on it. Its aim is moral, not historical: it gives almost no dates or names, and its chronology is disputed (most date it to around 530-545; Higham and others, earlier).

fuentes/de-excidio-britanniae/leer.0.tit.texto: English translation by J. A. Giles, Project Gutenberg

fuentes/piedra-de-vortiporio/resumen.texto: Funerary stone found at Castell Dwyran, in Carmarthenshire, with the Latin inscription MEMORIA VOTEPORIGIS PROTICTORIS, “memorial of Voteporix the protector,” a cross, and the name in ogham, VOTECORIGAS. Protector was a Roman military rank.

fuentes/piedra-de-vortiporio/por_que_imp.texto: If it is about King Vortiporius whom Gildas condemns, as many hold, it is the monument of a 6th-century king and shows the Roman heritage and the Irish presence in Dyfed; the identification is not certain.

fuentes/piedra-de-artognou/resumen.texto: Piece of slate found in 1998 at Tintagel, in a 6th-century context, reused in a drain, with a Latin inscription reading PATERN[...] COLI AVI FICIT ARTOGNOU, usually translated “Artognou, descendant of Patern... of Coll, made this.”

fuentes/piedra-de-artognou/por_que_impor.texto: The press called it “the stone of Arthur,” but Artognou is a different name and proves nothing about Arthur, as John Koch and others have pointed out; it does show that in 6th-century Cornwall there were people who wrote in Latin.

fuentes/vida-de-sanson/resumen.texto: Life of the Welsh monk Samson, a disciple of Illtud, who passed through Cornwall, where, according to the text, he converted people who performed rites around an idol and carved a cross on a stone, and who founded the monastery of Dol in Armorica. The author says he got his information from a relative of the saint.

fuentes/vida-de-sanson/por_que_importa.texto: It is the oldest surviving life of a British saint and a central source on emigration to Armorica; Robert Fawtier dated it to the 9th century and Pierre Flobert to the late 8th, while others hold to a 7th-century date.

fuentes/actas-del-segundo-concilio-de-br.texto: Acts of the Second Council of Braga

Acts of the council held in 572 in Braga, capital of the Suebic kingdom, presided over by Martin of Braga, with the canons approved and the signatures of the bishops. Among them signs Mailoc, bishop of the “Britonensian church,” the see of the Britons settled in northern Galicia.
It is, together with the Suebic Parrochiale, the documentary proof of the British community of Galicia.
Concilia Hispaniae (Patrologia Latina 84, Migne): the Second Council of Braga is in this volume (Wikisource)

fuentes/historia-brittonum/resumen.texto: Latin compilation written in Gwynedd around 829-830, in the time of King Merfyn Frych, which gathers the legendary origin of the Britons from the Trojan Brutus, Roman history, Vortigern and the arrival of Hengist and Horsa, the prophecy of the boy Ambrosius, the list of the twelve battles of Arthur, “leader of battles,” genealogies of Anglian and northern British kings, and a list of “wonders” of Britain. Some later manuscripts attribute it to a certain Nennius.

fuentes/historia-brittonum/por_que_impor.texto: It is the first source that makes Arthur a military leader, and a basis for Geoffrey of Monmouth. David Dumville showed that the attribution to Nennius is late and that the work is a politically motivated construction, not a faithful deposit of ancient traditions, so its value for the 5th century is very low.

fuentes/historia-brittonum/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by J. A. Giles, Project Gutenberg

fuentes/pilar-de-eliseg/titulo.texto: Inscription of the Pillar of Eliseg

fuentes/pilar-de-eliseg/autor.texto: Cyngen ap Cadell, king of Powys

fuentes/pilar-de-eliseg/resumen.texto: Stone column near Llangollen raised by Cyngen, king of Powys, in honor of his great-grandfather Eliseg, who recovered lands from the English. Its long Latin inscription, now almost illegible and known from the copy made by Edward Lhuyd in 1696, traces the genealogy of the kings of Powys back to Vortigern (Guarthigirn), blessed by Germanus, and Magnus Maximus, who “killed the king of the Romans.”

fuentes/pilar-de-eliseg/por_que_importa.texto: It is a political document of the 9th century that shows how a Welsh dynasty used Vortigern and Maximus as ancestors, the same tradition recorded in the Historia Brittonum.

fuentes/annales-cambriae/resumen.texto: Brief Latin chronicle probably compiled at St Davids in the mid-10th century and preserved in a manuscript of around 1100 alongside the Historia Brittonum. For 516 it records the battle of Badon, “in which Arthur carried the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ on his shoulders for three days and three nights,” and for 537 the battle of Camlann, “in which Arthur and Medraut fell.”

fuentes/annales-cambriae/por_que_importa.texto: It is the source of the two Arthurian dates and for that reason it has been at the center of the debate. Its 6th-century entries were partly taken from Irish chronicles and were added centuries later, so they do not prove that Arthur existed.

fuentes/vida-del-rey-alfredo/resumen.texto: Biography of King Alfred of Wessex written in 893 by Asser, a monk of St Davids who entered his service. It recounts the wars against the Vikings, the king's life and illnesses, and his program of learning; it says that the southern Welsh kings sought his protection against the sons of Rhodri Mawr, and it mentions the great dyke that Offa had built “from sea to sea.”

fuentes/vida-del-rey-alfredo/por_que_imp.texto: It is the first biography of an English king, written by a Welshman, and a source on relations between the Welsh kingdoms and Wessex; Alfred Smyth (1995) argued that it is a later forgery, but most accept it as authentic.

fuentes/y-gododdin/resumen.texto: Series of Welsh elegies mourning the warriors gathered by Mynyddog Mwynfawr, lord of Din Eidyn, who died attacking the Angles at Catraeth; each stanza praises the courage, generosity and death of a warrior who “paid for his mead.” It survives in a single manuscript, the Book of Aneirin, in two versions.

fuentes/y-gododdin/por_que_importa.texto: It may be the oldest poem in Welsh literature and the oldest composed in what is now Scotland. Ifor Williams and Kenneth Jackson attributed to it a core from around 600; David Dumville and others doubt that anything from that period survives, and John Koch proposed reconstructions of an original text that are much disputed. It contains the earliest possible mention of Arthur (“though he was not Arthur”), which may be an interpolation.

fuentes/libro-de-taliesin/resumen.texto: Welsh manuscript from the first half of the 14th century with some sixty poems attributed to Taliesin: songs of praise to Urien of Rheged, to his son Owain and to Cynan Garwyn of Powys, prophetic poems such as Armes Prydein, religious poems, and others on legendary themes, such as Preiddeu Annwfn, the expedition of Arthur to the otherworld.

fuentes/libro-de-taliesin/por_que_import.texto: Ifor Williams separated a dozen poems that may be from the historical Taliesin of the 6th century, which would make them among the oldest texts in a Celtic language of Britain; the dating of that core is disputed. The rest shows the legendary figure of the poet who knows everything.

fuentes/libro-de-taliesin/leer.0.titulo.texto: “The Four Ancient Books of Wales”, vol. 2, W. F. Skene (1868), with Welsh texts and translation, Internet Archive

fuentes/armes-prydein/resumen.texto: Prophetic poem preserved in the Book of Taliesin that announces that the Welsh, allied with the Irish, the Norse of Dublin, the people of Cornwall, the Bretons and the northern Britons, will expel the English and the tax collectors of their king from the whole island, guided by the heroes Cynan and Cadwaladr.

fuentes/armes-prydein/por_que_importa.texto: It is often dated to around 930-940 and read as a protest against the submission of Hywel Dda to Athelstan, a date that some dispute; it is the clearest evidence of a shared consciousness among the British peoples facing the English.

fuentes/mabinogi/titulo.texto: The Four Branches of the Mabinogi

fuentes/mabinogi/soporte.texto: White Book of Rhydderch (around 1350) and Red Book of Hergest (around 1382-1410), with fragments in manuscript Peniarth 6 (13th century)

fuentes/mabinogi/resumen.texto: Four Welsh prose tales (Pwyll, Branwen, Manawydan and Math) about Pwyll, lord of Dyfed, Rhiannon, the giant Bendigeidfran and his sister Branwen, married to a king of Ireland, the magician Gwydion and Lleu. They survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (around 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (late 14th or early 15th century), and in fragments of Branwen and Manawydan from the mid-13th century, alongside other tales that Charlotte Guest translated in 1838-1849 under the name Mabinogion.

fuentes/mabinogi/por_que_importa.texto: It is the great work of medieval Welsh prose. The date of composition is disputed: Thomas Charles-Edwards (1970) proposed between 1050 and 1120, and others, such as Saunders Lewis, placed it in the late 12th century. It is also debated how much it preserves of an earlier mythology (some characters bear the names of gods, such as Rhiannon, from Rigantona, or Lleu, from Lugus) and how much is the creation of an 11th- or 12th-century author writing for his own world; Sioned Davies and others stress its own narrative art.

fuentes/mabinogi/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by Charlotte Guest (Mabinogion), Project Gutenberg

fuentes/culhwch-y-olwen/resumen.texto: Welsh prose tale in which the young Culhwch, to marry Olwen, daughter of the giant Ysbaddaden, asks help from his cousin Arthur, who with his warriors (Cei, Bedwyr and a long list of names) carries out a series of impossible tasks, among them the hunt for the boar Twrch Trwyth across Wales, Cornwall and Ireland.

fuentes/culhwch-y-olwen/por_que_importa.texto: It is the oldest prose Arthurian tale, earlier than Geoffrey of Monmouth, and it shows a folktale Arthur, leader of a band of heroes with magical powers; it is one of Padel's arguments for seeing Arthur as a figure of legend rather than of history.

fuentes/culhwch-y-olwen/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by Charlotte Guest (Mabinogion), Project Gutenberg

fuentes/leyes-de-hywel-dda/resumen.texto: Medieval Welsh law, preserved in about forty manuscripts from the 13th to the 16th centuries, in Welsh and in Latin, in three main recensions (Cyfnerth, Blegywryd and Iorwerth). Their prologues say that Hywel Dda gathered at Whitland six men from each cantref to revise the laws; they deal with the king's court, the price of each person's blood (galanas), marriage and divorce, land and the rights of women.

fuentes/leyes-de-hywel-dda/por_que_impor.texto: It is the main source on medieval Welsh society and was a symbol of identity against English law. The attribution to Hywel is a tradition that gave authority to texts that were rewritten until the 13th century.

fuentes/leyes-de-hywel-dda/leer.0.titulo.texto: “Ancient Laws and Institutes of Wales”, A. Owen (1841), Internet Archive

fuentes/brut-y-tywysogion/resumen.texto: Welsh chronicle that follows the history of Wales year by year from 682, where Geoffrey of Monmouth's History ends, to 1282. It survives in several Welsh versions translated from a lost Latin chronicle, probably written in the Cistercian monastery of Strata Florida.

fuentes/brut-y-tywysogion/por_que_import.texto: It is the main Welsh narrative source on the princes and on the conquest by Edward I, written from the Welsh side.

fuentes/brut-y-tywysogion/leer.0.titulo.texto: “Brut y Tywysogion”, edition and translation by J. Williams ab Ithel (1860), Internet Archive

fuentes/estatuto-de-rhuddlan/resumen.texto: Ordinance issued by Edward I at Rhuddlan Castle in March 1284, which incorporated the principality of Wales into the English crown, divided it into counties with sheriffs on the English model, and imposed English criminal law, while keeping Welsh law in force in some civil matters.

fuentes/estatuto-de-rhuddlan/por_que_imp.texto: It is the document of the annexation of Wales, which governed until the Laws in Wales Acts of 1535-1542.

fuentes/estatuto-de-rhuddlan/leer.0.titu.texto: “The Statutes of Wales” by I. Bowen (1908), with the Statutum Walliae in English (Wikisource)

fuentes/descripcion-de-gales/resumen.texto: Description of Wales and the Welsh in two books: the first, their virtues (hospitality, singing in several voices, courage, sharpness of speech); the second, their defects (inconstancy, theft, disputes over land), with advice to the English on how to conquer them and to the Welsh on how to resist. It ends with the reply of an old Welshman to Henry II: no other people will answer for this corner of the earth on the day of Judgment.

fuentes/descripcion-de-gales/por_que_imp.texto: It is a portrait of a Celtic people written by someone who half belonged to it, with an unusual balance between praise and criticism.

fuentes/descripcion-de-gales/leer.0.titu.texto: “Historical Works of Giraldus Cambrensis”, Hoare translation (1905 edition), Internet Archive

fuentes/confesion-de-patricio/soporte.texto: Manuscripts (the oldest, in the Book of Armagh, around 807)

fuentes/confesion-de-patricio/resumen.texto: Autobiographical text written in Latin by Patrick in his old age to defend himself against accusations from his superiors in Britain. He says he was the son of the deacon Calpurnius, from a villa near Bannavem Taburniae; that at sixteen he was captured by Irish pirates; that he spent six years as a slave tending livestock; that he escaped and, after a vision, returned as a bishop to preach among the Irish, amid baptisms, gifts to kings and dangers. He apologizes for his rustic Latin.

fuentes/confesion-de-patricio/por_que_im.texto: Together with the Letter to Coroticus, it is the only text written in 5th-century Ireland and the only direct testimony of Patrick; almost everything that tradition added later (Tara, the shamrock, the snakes) is not in it. Its authenticity is not disputed; its date and the places it names are.

fuentes/confesion-de-patricio/leer.0.tit.texto: Works of Saint Patrick (Confessio and Letter to Coroticus) in Latin, Project Gutenberg

fuentes/confesion-de-patricio/leer.1.tit.texto: Latin text, Royal Irish Academy edition (St. Patrick's Confessio)

fuentes/confesion-de-patricio/leer.2.tit.texto: English translation, Royal Irish Academy (St. Patrick's Confessio)

fuentes/carta-a-corotico/titulo.texto: Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus

fuentes/carta-a-corotico/resumen.texto: Open letter from Patrick excommunicating the soldiers of Coroticus, a Christian British chieftain, who had killed newly baptized neophytes and sold others as slaves to the Scots and to the “apostate Picts.” Patrick demands that they return the captives and presents himself as a foreigner exiled for the love of God.

fuentes/carta-a-corotico/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the slave trade between Ireland and Britain and the existence of Christian British kingdoms in the 5th century; the identification of Coroticus with Ceretic, king of Alt Clut, is traditional and disputed.

fuentes/carta-a-corotico/leer.0.titulo.texto: Works of Saint Patrick (Confessio and Letter to Coroticus) in Latin, Project Gutenberg

fuentes/carta-a-corotico/leer.1.titulo.texto: English translation, Royal Irish Academy (St. Patrick's Confessio)

fuentes/vida-de-patricio-muirchu/resumen.texto: Life of Patrick written at the end of the 7th century and preserved in the Book of Armagh. It tells of his capture, his training in Gaul, his dispatch after the failure of Palladius, the Easter when he lit a fire at Slane before King Lóegaire's fire at Tara, his miracle contests with the druids, the conversion of kings and his death at Saul.

fuentes/vida-de-patricio-muirchu/por_que.texto: It is the basis of the traditional Patrick, constructed two centuries after him to support the primacy of Armagh; its value for the 5th century is slight, but it shows how the 7th-century Church imagined the conversion.

fuentes/vida-de-patricio-muirchu/leer.0..texto: “The Tripartite Life of Patrick”, ed. W. Stokes (1887): includes Muirchú’s Life in Latin, Internet Archive

fuentes/vida-de-brigida-cogitoso/resumen.texto: The oldest surviving Irish hagiography: a series of miracles of Brigid involving milk, food, livestock and healing. It ends with a description of the great wooden church of Kildare, divided for men and women, with the tombs of Brigid and of Bishop Conlaed.

fuentes/vida-de-brigida-cogitoso/por_que.texto: It shows Kildare's ambition to be the head of the Irish Church against Armagh, and it is one of the few texts that describe a 7th-century Irish building.

fuentes/vida-de-columba-adomnan/resumen.texto: Life of Columba written by the ninth abbot of Iona, a century after the saint's death, in three books: prophecies, miracles and visions. Among the episodes are the visit to the Pictish king Bridei and his magician Broichan, the “ordination” of King Áedán mac Gabráin, the encounter with a beast in the River Ness, and many details of daily life in the monastery.

fuentes/vida-de-columba-adomnan/por_que_.texto: It is the main source on Iona, Irish monasticism and the 6th-century Picts, written by someone who knew the community from within, although with the aims of a hagiography. Its oldest manuscript, from around 700, is preserved in Schaffhausen.

fuentes/vida-de-columba-adomnan/leer.0.t.texto: English translation on CELT (University College Cork)

fuentes/anales-de-ulster/autor.texto: Cathal Óg Mac Maghnusa and earlier compilers

fuentes/anales-de-ulster/resumen.texto: Year-by-year chronicle of Ireland from 431 to 1540, compiled at the end of the 15th century in Fermanagh from earlier chronicles. Its early entries derive from a chronicle kept at Iona from the late 6th or 7th century, and then from another from central Ireland; they record the deaths of kings and abbots, battles, Viking attacks and natural phenomena.

fuentes/anales-de-ulster/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most reliable Irish chronicle for the early Middle Ages and the source for much of the history of Dál Riata and of the Picts. The entries of the 5th century and the early 6th are later reconstructions and are used with care.

fuentes/anales-de-ulster/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation on CELT (University College Cork)

fuentes/libro-de-armagh/autor.texto: Ferdomnach of Armagh and other scribes

fuentes/libro-de-armagh/resumen.texto: Manuscript copied at Armagh around 807, largely by the scribe Ferdomnach, which brings together the texts on Patrick (the Confessio, the Life by Muirchú, the notes of Tírechán and documents on the properties of Armagh), a complete New Testament and the Life of Martin of Tours by Sulpicius Severus. In 1005 a note was added in which Brian Boru is called “emperor of the Irish.”

fuentes/libro-de-armagh/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most important manuscript for the history of Patrick and of Armagh's claims to primacy. It is kept at Trinity College Dublin.

fuentes/libro-de-armagh/leer.0.titulo.texto: “Liber Ardmachanus. The Book of Armagh”, ed. J. Gwynn (1913), Internet Archive

fuentes/cathach-de-columba/resumen.texto: Fragmentary Latin psalter from the late 6th or early 7th century, the oldest surviving Irish manuscript and one of the first examples of insular script, with decorated initials. The O'Donnell family carried it into battle as a talisman (cathach, “the fighter”), and legend says it is the copy that Columba made in secret from a book of Finnian's.

fuentes/cathach-de-columba/por_que_impor.texto: It is the starting point of insular calligraphy and illumination; the attribution to Columba's hand is traditional and cannot be proved. It is kept at the Royal Irish Academy.

fuentes/tablillas-de-springmount/resumen.texto: Six yew-wood tablets covered in wax, found in a bog in Antrim in 1913-1914, with Psalms 30 to 32 written in Latin, probably by a pupil learning to write.

fuentes/tablillas-de-springmount/por_que.texto: They are among the oldest written texts from Ireland and show how reading and writing were taught in monastic schools.

fuentes/libro-de-durrow/resumen.texto: Latin gospel book from around 650-700, the oldest of the great complete insular illuminated books, with “carpet” pages covered in interlace, the symbols of the evangelists and large decorated initials. It was kept at the monastery of Durrow, founded by Columba.

fuentes/libro-de-durrow/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the mixture of La Tène, Germanic and Mediterranean motifs in insular art, a century before the Book of Kells; it is debated whether it was made in Ireland, Iona or Northumbria, a debate mixed with national pride.

fuentes/glosas-de-wurzburgo/resumen.texto: Manuscript of Paul's letters with more than 3,500 glosses in Old Irish and Latin, written between the lines and in the margins around the mid-8th century. It is kept in the university library of Würzburg, where Irish monks brought it.

fuentes/glosas-de-wurzburgo/por_que_impo.texto: Together with the Milan and St Gall glosses, it is the basis of knowledge of Old Irish; Johann Kaspar Zeuss used them in his Grammatica Celtica of 1853 to show that Irish is an Indo-European language related to Welsh and Gaulish.

fuentes/glosas-de-wurzburgo/leer.0.titul.texto: “Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus”, vol. 1, Stokes and Strachan (1901), Internet Archive

fuentes/inscripciones-ogamicas/resumen.texto: About four hundred stones with ogham inscriptions, an alphabet of strokes set against a line (the edge of the stone), most of them in southern Ireland (Kerry, Cork, Waterford) and others in Wales, Cornwall, the Isle of Man and Scotland. Almost all are names in the genitive with the formula “of X son of Y” (X MAQI Y), probably grave or property markers; in Wales many are bilingual, with Latin.

fuentes/inscripciones-ogamicas/por_que_i.texto: They are the oldest texts in a Goidelic language: the first stones are dated by their language to around the 4th century, and most are from the 5th and 6th centuries. Damian McManus (1991) holds that the alphabet was invented in Ireland by people who knew the classification of letters by Latin grammarians; Eoin MacNeill and James Carney (1975) saw it as a secret script created in response to Roman Britain, and Carney even proposed, without evidence, the 1st century BC. The medieval tradition attributed it to Ogma. The Scottish stones with Pictish ogham are poorly read and have fed the idea of a non-Indo-European language.

fuentes/inscripciones-ogamicas/leer.0.ti.texto: Ogham in 3D: corpus of stones with models and readings (Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies)

fuentes/auraicept-na-n-eces/resumen.texto: Irish grammatical treatise, with a core from the 7th or 8th century and much later commentaries, which compares Irish grammar with Latin. It says that Fénius Farsaid created the Irish language at the Tower of Babel from the best of all languages, explains ogham and its invention, and gives lists of secret ogham alphabets.

fuentes/auraicept-na-n-eces/por_que_impo.texto: It is the main medieval source on ogham and shows how Irish scholars defended their language against Latin. Its account of origins is a learned construction, not an ancient tradition.

fuentes/auraicept-na-n-eces/leer.0.titul.texto: “Auraicept na n-Éces”, edition and translation by G. Calder (1917), Internet Archive

fuentes/senchas-mar/resumen.texto: The largest collection of Irish legal treatises, some fifty texts gathered in the 8th century on the status of persons, contracts, clientship, marriage, pledges, kinship and other topics, with abundant glosses and later commentaries. Its prologue says that Patrick had the laws revised by a commission of nine, together with the poet Dubthach.

fuentes/senchas-mar/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main source on early medieval Irish society: hierarchical, rural and without cities, with kings of small kingdoms (túatha), clients, kin groups and professional jurists. It is debated how much it preserves of pre-Christian law and how much it owes to canon law; current research (Liam Breatnach, Fergus Kelly) stresses the influence of the Church.

fuentes/senchas-mar/leer.0.titulo.texto: “Ancient Laws of Ireland” (Senchus Mór), vol. 1 (1865), Internet Archive

fuentes/crith-gablach/resumen.texto: Legal treatise from the early 8th century on the grades of Irish society, from the child and the client up to the king: for each it gives the house, the livestock, the food to which the person is entitled as a guest, the retinue and the “honor price” to be paid if he is offended. It also describes the king's week: Sunday for drinking, Monday for judging, and so on.

fuentes/crith-gablach/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most detailed description of the Irish social hierarchy; it is an ideal scheme of jurists, not a portrait of reality, and it is debated how closely it matched practice.

fuentes/audacht-morainn/resumen.texto: Advice that the legendary judge Morann sends to the future king Feradach: through the “truth of the ruler” (fír flathemon) come peace, good harvests, abundant milk, fish in the rivers and healthy children; through injustice, famine and war.

fuentes/audacht-morainn/por_que_importa.texto: It is the oldest Irish “mirror for princes,” edited by Fergus Kelly in 1976; the idea that the king's justice brings the fertility of the land is debated, either as a pre-Christian inheritance or as an echo of the Old Testament.

fuentes/audacht-morainn/leer.0.titulo.texto: Audacht Morainn in the Book of Leinster (CELT, University College Cork)

fuentes/cain-adomnain/resumen.texto: Law promulgated at the synod of Birr in 697 that forbids killing or harming women, children and clerics in war and sets fines for offenders, payable to the community of Iona. The surviving text adds a later introduction on the hard life of women before the law and the list of the 91 guarantors, among them Irish kings, the king of Dál Riata and the Pictish king Bridei.

fuentes/cain-adomnain/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the first European laws to protect non-combatants, and the list of guarantors is a unique document on the kingdoms of 697.

fuentes/cain-adomnain/leer.0.titulo.texto: “Cáin Adamnáin”, edition and translation by K. Meyer (1905), Internet Archive

fuentes/tain-bo-cuailnge/resumen.texto: The great saga of the Ulster Cycle: Queen Medb and King Ailill of Connacht invade Ulster to seize the brown bull of Cooley, and while the warriors of Ulster lie prostrate under a curse, the young Cú Chulainn holds them off alone in a series of single combats, until he kills his foster brother Fer Diad. The first version, whose oldest language dates from the 8th century, survives in the Lebor na hUidre and the Yellow Book of Lecan; the second, more polished, in the Book of Leinster.

fuentes/tain-bo-cuailnge/por_que_importa.texto: Kenneth Jackson (1964) read it as “a window on the Iron Age,” preserving the world of chariots, severed heads and feasts that Posidonius and the Greeks describe. James Carney (1955) and later Kim McCone (1990) argued that it is a literary creation of Christian scholars who knew the Bible and Latin literature, and J. P. Mallory (2016) showed that its material culture is almost entirely that of the early Middle Ages; the copyist of the Book of Leinster himself warned that some things were “deceits of demons” and others “poetic inventions.”

fuentes/tain-bo-cuailnge/leer.0.titulo.texto: First version, English translation by Cecile O'Rahilly on CELT

fuentes/tain-bo-cuailnge/leer.1.titulo.texto: Version of the Book of Leinster, English translation on CELT

fuentes/togail-bruidne-da-derga/titulo.texto: The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel

fuentes/togail-bruidne-da-derga/resumen.texto: Saga of King Conaire Mór of Tara, who breaks one after another his geissi (ritual prohibitions) and dies when raiders attack the hospitality house of Da Derga where he is staying; much of the tale is the description of the warriors a spy sees inside the house.

fuentes/togail-bruidne-da-derga/por_que_.texto: It is one of the favorite sources of those who look in the sagas for pre-Christian sacred kingship; for anti-nativist critics, its themes are explained by biblical culture and the politics of the 8th to 11th centuries.

fuentes/togail-bruidne-da-derga/leer.0.t.texto: “Togail Bruidne Da Derga”, edition and translation by W. Stokes (1902), Internet Archive

fuentes/immram-brain/resumen.texto: Short prose and verse tale in which Bran mac Febail, invited by a woman from the otherworld, sails to wonderful islands, meets Manannán, god of the sea, who announces to him the birth of Christ, and reaches the Island of Women; on his return, one of his companions sets foot on land and turns to ashes, because centuries had passed.

fuentes/immram-brain/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the oldest Irish texts and the model of the otherworld voyages; it mixes pre-Christian and Christian themes and was central to the debate on the continuity of tradition.

fuentes/immram-brain/leer.0.titulo.texto: “The Voyage of Bran”, edition and translation by K. Meyer (1895), Internet Archive

fuentes/navegacion-de-san-brendan/resume.texto: Latin account of the voyage of Brendan and fourteen monks for seven years across the ocean in search of the “promised land of the saints”: they celebrate Easter on the back of a whale, find a pillar of crystal, an island of smiths who hurl fire at them, and Judas on a rock.

fuentes/navegacion-de-san-brendan/por_qu.texto: It was one of the most widely read texts in medieval Europe. Some see in it memories of real voyages by Irish monks to the Faroes and Iceland, which the geographer Dicuil confirms around 825; Tim Severin repeated the voyage in a leather boat in 1976-1977 to show that it was possible to reach America, which does not prove that Brendan did so.

fuentes/lebor-na-huidre/autor.texto: Máel Muire mac Céilechair and other scribes

fuentes/lebor-na-huidre/resumen.texto: The oldest surviving manuscript written almost entirely in Irish, copied at Clonmacnoise around 1100; one of its scribes, Máel Muire mac Céilechair, died there in 1106. It contains, incomplete, the first version of the Táin, the Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel, the Feast of Bricriu, otherworld voyages and religious texts; tradition said it was written on the hide of Ciarán's cow.

fuentes/lebor-na-huidre/por_que_importa.texto: It is a foundation for the study of early Irish literature and shows how monks of a great monastery gathered and rewrote the sagas. It is kept at the Royal Irish Academy.

fuentes/libro-de-leinster/autor.texto: Áed Ua Crimthainn and other scribes

fuentes/libro-de-leinster/resumen.texto: Large 12th-century Irish manuscript, compiled largely by Áed Ua Crimthainn, abbot of Terryglass. It brings together the second version of the Táin, the Lebor Gabála, the Dindshenchas, genealogies, king lists, poems and sagas from all the cycles.

fuentes/libro-de-leinster/por_que_import.texto: It is the broadest collection of medieval Irish tradition. At the end of the Táin, a copyist wrote in Latin that he did not believe that story, because some things were “deceits of demons,” others “poetic inventions,” and others were made “for the delight of fools”: a testimony of how its own copyists saw it.

fuentes/libro-de-leinster/leer.0.titulo.texto: Book of Leinster (CELT, University College Cork)

fuentes/acallam-na-senorach/resumen.texto: The greatest work of the Finn Cycle: the warriors Caílte and Oisín, who survived their leader Finn mac Cumaill by centuries, travel through Ireland with Patrick and tell him the stories of each place, in prose with interspersed poems; Patrick listens to them, blesses them and has their tales written down.

fuentes/acallam-na-senorach/por_que_impo.texto: It is the greatest medieval Irish narrative work and a clear example of how 12th-century Christian scholars reconciled the pagan past with faith; it is a central work of the Fenian tradition, the same as the Gaelic ballads of Scotland that Macpherson reworked in his own way in Ossian.

fuentes/acallam-na-senorach/leer.0.titul.texto: W. Stokes edition, “Irische Texte” (1900) (CELT, University College Cork)

fuentes/piedras-con-simbolos-pictos/resu.texto: About three hundred and fifty stones from eastern and northern Scotland with recurring symbols (the crescent with a V-rod, the double disc with a Z-rod, the “Pictish beast,” the mirror and comb, animals), which appear only in Pictish territory. The oldest are unworked slabs with incised symbols; the later ones are Christian crosses in relief with symbols and scenes, such as the Aberlemno stone with a battle.

fuentes/piedras-con-simbolos-pictos/por_.texto: They are the main own testimony of the Picts, who left almost no texts. Their meaning is unknown: it has been proposed that they are names, lineages, ranks or a writing system (Lee, Jonathan and Ziman, 2010, a much-disputed idea), and their chronology is also debated.

fuentes/piedras-con-simbolos-pictos/leer.texto: “The Early Christian Monuments of Scotland”, J. Romilly Allen and J. Anderson (1903), Internet Archive

fuentes/lista-de-reyes-pictos/resumen.texto: Lists of the kings of the Picts with the length of their reigns, preserved in several versions in later Scottish and Irish manuscripts; they begin with legendary kings (Cruithne and his seven sons, eponyms of the provinces) and continue with historical kings down to the 9th century. Many kings appear as sons of a father who was not a king, which fed the idea of succession through the female line.

fuentes/lista-de-reyes-pictos/por_que_im.texto: They are the backbone of Pictish history, although they were copied and reworked by Gaelic scribes. The matrilineal succession, which Bede also mentions, is debated: Alex Woolf and others see it as a construction of the scholars themselves.

fuentes/lista-de-reyes-pictos/leer.0.tit.texto: “Chronicles of the Picts, Chronicles of the Scots”, W. F. Skene (1867), Internet Archive

fuentes/senchus-fer-n-alban/titulo.texto: History of the Men of Alba

fuentes/senchus-fer-n-alban/resumen.texto: Text that gathers genealogies of the kings of Dál Riata and a kind of military census of its three great lineages: according to it, the Cenél nGabráin had 560 households, the Cenél nÓengusa 430 and the Cenél Loairn 420, and every twenty households had to provide two ships with seven rowing benches. It survives in a 10th-century version probably based on a 7th-century document.

fuentes/senchus-fer-n-alban/por_que_impo.texto: It is the oldest administrative document from Scotland and one of the few early medieval sources with population figures; it counts households and military obligations, not inhabitants, and how complete it is is not known.

fuentes/laudabiliter/resumen.texto: Bull attributed to Pope Adrian IV, the only English pope, which authorizes King Henry II to enter Ireland to “extend the boundaries of the Church” and correct the vices of its people, in exchange for an annual tribute to Rome. Its text is known only through Giraldus Cambrensis, who copied it decades later, and through a mention by John of Salisbury.

fuentes/laudabiliter/por_que_importa.texto: It was used to justify the Anglo-Norman conquest of Ireland, and for that reason its authenticity has been debated for centuries; most historians accept that there was a papal grant, but not that Giraldus's text is faithful.

fuentes/topografia-de-irlanda/resumen.texto: Description of Ireland that Giraldus wrote after his 1185 journey and read aloud in Oxford: its geography and animals, its marvels and miracles, and the history and customs of its inhabitants, whom he calls a “barbarous people” that lives “like beasts,” although he praises their music.

fuentes/topografia-de-irlanda/por_que_im.texto: It is a classic of the colonial gaze: it served to justify the conquest and its prejudices were repeated for centuries; in the 17th century John Lynch refuted it point by point in Cambrensis Eversus.

fuentes/topografia-de-irlanda/leer.0.tit.texto: “Historical Works of Giraldus Cambrensis”, Forester translation (1905 edition), Internet Archive

fuentes/expugnacion-de-irlanda/resumen.texto: History of the arrival of the Anglo-Normans in Ireland from the expulsion of Diarmait Mac Murchada in 1166 to 1185, written by a relative of several of the conquerors, the FitzGeralds and the FitzStephens, whom it presents as heroes; it includes the text of the bull Laudabiliter.

fuentes/expugnacion-de-irlanda/por_que_i.texto: It is the main narrative source on the invasion, written from the conquerors' side and with family and political aims.

fuentes/expugnacion-de-irlanda/leer.0.ti.texto: “Historical Works of Giraldus Cambrensis”, Forester translation (1905 edition), Internet Archive

fuentes/iron-age-communities-in-britain/.texto: Synthesis of the British Iron Age, reissued and updated through its fourth edition of 2005, which divides the island into regions with different developments: the south dominated by hillforts, east Yorkshire with the Arras burials, the north with brochs, and the southeast in contact with Gaul. It proposes that hillforts became central places for storage and redistribution.

It is the reference work on the period. Its model of hierarchical hillforts and of “tribes” with fixed territories was criticized by J. D. Hill and others for projecting Roman sources and a centralized order onto more diverse societies.

fuentes/ritual-and-rubbish-hill/titulo.texto: Ritual and Rubbish in the Iron Age of Wessex

fuentes/ritual-and-rubbish-hill/resumen.texto: Study of the deposits in pits and ditches of Wessex settlements, showing that objects, animals and human remains were not discarded at random but according to rules, in deposits with a ritual meaning. Hill criticizes the image of a homogeneous and hierarchical “Celtic” society taken from the classical authors.

fuentes/ritual-and-rubbish-hill/por_que_.texto: It changed the way British sites were read and promoted the idea of studying the Iron Age of Britain without the mold of Caesar's “Celts”; it is criticized for attributing a ritual meaning that is hard to prove to almost everything found in a pit.

fuentes/maiden-castle-wheeler/resumen.texto: Report of the excavations Wheeler directed in 1934-1937 at the great hillfort in Dorset, with its sequence from the Neolithic and the description of a “war cemetery” with dozens of burials, some with wounds, which he interpreted as the victims of the assault of Vespasian's legion in 43-44.

fuentes/maiden-castle-wheeler/por_que_im.texto: Wheeler's account, written with drama, became the classic image of the Roman conquest. Niall Sharples (1991) showed that the cemetery was used over a period of time, that only a few of the dead had wounds, and that there is no evidence of an assault; the projectile point lodged in a vertebra may date from another time.

fuentes/towers-in-the-north-armit/titulo.texto: Towers in the North: The Brochs of Scotland

fuentes/towers-in-the-north-armit/resume.texto: Armit gathers what is known about the brochs and argues that they arose in northern and western Scotland as a local development of the thick-walled round houses (the “Atlantic roundhouses” of the first millennium BC), as residences of important families, and not as fortresses of invaders arriving from the south, as was previously thought.

fuentes/towers-in-the-north-armit/por_qu.texto: It sums up the current consensus on the local origin of the brochs; their fine chronology and their function remain under discussion.

fuentes/iron-age-cemeteries-in-east-york.texto: Iron Age Cemeteries in East Yorkshire
Report of Ian Stead's excavations at the cemeteries of Burton Fleming, Rudston and Garton-Wetwang, with hundreds of Arras culture graves under square-ditched barrows, some with chariots.

It is the basis for the study of the Arras culture; Stead stressed the differences from the chariot burials of Champagne (here the chariot was dismantled and the dead person was flexed), which weakened the idea of a simple invasion from Gaul.

fuentes/early-celtic-art-in-the-british-.texto: Early Celtic Art in the British Isles

Catalogue and study, in two volumes published after the death of Martyn Jope, of the objects decorated in La Tène style found in Britain and Ireland: shields, mirrors, helmets, scabbards, torcs, harness fittings and carved stones.
It is the reference corpus of insular Iron Age art. Its stylistic chronology, based on comparisons with the continent, is debated because few objects are securely dated.

fuentes/an-imperial-possession/titulo.texto: An Imperial Possession: Britain in the Roman Empire, 54 BC - AD 409

fuentes/an-imperial-possession/resumen.texto: History of Roman Britain from postcolonial theory: Mattingly argues that Rome was a colonial power that exploited the province, that “Romanization” benefited a minority, and that different identities (military, urban, rural) coexisted in Britain rather than a single Romano-British culture.

fuentes/an-imperial-possession/por_que_i.texto: It changed the traditional approach, which saw the conquest as a civilizing enterprise. Its critics point out that it exaggerates exploitation and resistance, and that the same evidence admits a reading of voluntary integration of the elites.

fuentes/boudica-hingley-unwin/resumen.texto: Study that separates what is known about Boudica (two brief accounts by Tacitus, one by Cassius Dio, and the layers of destruction) from what was built later: the Boadicea of the Tudor period, the imperial Victorian heroine of the Westminster statue, the feminist and nationalist symbol.

fuentes/boudica-hingley-unwin/por_que_im.texto: It shows that the historical Boudica is almost unknown and that her image changed according to the needs of each era; it is an example of reception history, which some consider more useful for understanding modern Britons than the Iceni.

fuentes/language-and-history-in-early-br.texto: Language and History in Early Britain

Study of the evolution of the Brittonic languages, from the British of the Roman period to Welsh, Cornish and Breton, between the 1st and 12th centuries, with a chronology of sound changes based on inscriptions, place names and loanwords from Latin and into English. It includes a map of rivers with British names showing the Anglo-Saxon advance from east to west.

For half a century it was the reference on the language of the Britons and the emigration to Brittany; its chronology was later revised (Sims-Williams, 2003), and its model of Anglo-Saxon advance, tied to the narrative of a conquest, is now debated with archaeology and genetics.

fuentes/arthurs-britain-alcock/titulo.texto: Arthur's Britain: History and Archaeology AD 367-634

fuentes/arthurs-britain-alcock/resumen.texto: Synthesis of post-Roman Britain combining written sources and archaeology, including Alcock's own excavations at Cadbury Castle and Dinas Powys. Alcock accepted the entries of the Annales Cambriae as evidence that Arthur was a real military leader in the early 6th century.

fuentes/arthurs-britain-alcock/por_que_i.texto: It was the most influential work of the “historicist” current. Dumville (1977) criticized its use of late sources as if they were contemporary, and Alcock himself later moderated his position.

fuentes/sub-roman-britain-dumville/resum.texto: Dumville examines the sources for 5th- and 6th-century Britain and shows that the Historia Brittonum and the Annales Cambriae are late constructions that do not allow the reconstruction of events or figures of that period. On Arthur he concludes that there is no historical evidence and that he should be removed from the history books.

fuentes/sub-roman-britain-dumville/por_q.texto: It marked the skeptical turn in British historiography; its critics reproach it for a skepticism that leaves the period without possible history, but its critique of the sources is broadly accepted.

fuentes/the-nature-of-arthur-padel/resum.texto: Padel studies the earliest Welsh mentions of Arthur, the place names associated with him, and tales such as Culhwch and Olwen, and argues that Arthur was first a folklore hero, a monster-hunter and leader of a band of warriors in a magical world, who was later historicized, as other legendary heroes were.

fuentes/the-nature-of-arthur-padel/por_q.texto: It is the most cited argument against a historical Arthur; historicists reply that a real person could become legendary, and the debate continues without new sources.

fuentes/worlds-of-arthur-halsall/titulo.texto: Worlds of Arthur: Facts and Fictions of the Dark Ages

fuentes/worlds-of-arthur-halsall/resumen.texto: Halsall reviews the written sources and the archaeology of 5th- and 6th-century Britain and concludes that it cannot be known whether Arthur existed, and that the sources cannot be used to reconstruct a narrative of battles. He proposes that the arrival of the Anglo-Saxons was earlier, tied to the crisis of the Empire, and without a great violent conquest.

fuentes/worlds-of-arthur-halsall/por_que.texto: It is a recent synthesis of the critical approach, against Arthur-seekers and against the traditional narrative of the invasion; some of his hypotheses about the Saxon arrival are disputed.

fuentes/language-in-pictland-forsyth/tit.texto: Language in Pictland: The Case Against 'Non-Indo-European Pictish'

fuentes/language-in-pictland-forsyth/res.texto: Brief study that reviews Kenneth Jackson's thesis (1955), according to which two languages were spoken in the Pictish kingdom, a Brittonic one and a non-Indo-European and earlier one, which would explain the unintelligible ogham inscriptions. Forsyth shows that these inscriptions are hard because of their state of preservation and their abbreviations, not because of the language, and that Pictish place names and personal names are Brittonic.

fuentes/language-in-pictland-forsyth/por.texto: Her conclusion, that Pictish was a Brittonic Celtic language related to Welsh, is now the majority view (Guto Rhys, Simon Taylor); the inscriptions still lack a complete translation, and some keep doubts about an earlier substrate.

fuentes/genomas-pictos-morez-2023/titulo.texto: Imputed genomes and haplotype-based analyses of the Picts of early medieval Scotland reveal fine-scale relatedness between Iron Age, early medieval and the modern people of the UK

fuentes/genomas-pictos-morez-2023/resume.texto: Analysis of ancient DNA from eight individuals from two Pictish cemeteries of the 5th to 7th centuries (Lundin Links, in Fife, and Balintore, in Easter Ross), with two complete good-quality genomes compared with more than 8,300 ancient and modern genomes. It concludes that the Picts belonged to the genetic makeup of the British Iron Age, that those of the Orkneys were distinct from those of the continent, and that the Picts of the continent share more DNA segments with the present-day population of western Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland and Northumbria than with that of eastern Scotland, where the center of their kingdom was. The seven mitochondrial DNAs from Lundin Links show no common maternal lineages, which the authors read as an argument against the idea of a matrilineal society.

fuentes/genomas-pictos-morez-2023/por_qu.texto: It contradicts with genetic data the exotic origins attributed to the Picts (Scythia according to Bede, a prehistoric non-Indo-European people according to others) and supports a local origin; the sample is very small, the argument on matrilineality is indirect, and the study says nothing direct about their language.

fuentes/genomas-pictos-morez-2023/leer.0.texto: Full article in open access (PLOS Genetics)

fuentes/were-the-scots-irish-campbell/re.texto: Campbell argues that the archaeology of Argyll shows no arrival of an Irish population around 500 (the houses, forts and objects follow local traditions), and that the account of a migration from Antrim is a later genealogical construction; he proposes that Gaelic was spoken in Argyll from the Iron Age.

fuentes/were-the-scots-irish-campbell/po.texto: It opened a debate that continues: most accept that the account of Fergus Mór is late, but many historians and linguists see evidence of a Gaelic expansion from Ireland at some point.

fuentes/from-pictland-to-alba-woolf/resu.texto: History of northern Britain from the first Viking attacks to the 11th century, which explains the disappearance of the Picts and the birth of the kingdom of Alba as a long process, marked by the defeat of 839 at the hands of the Vikings and the Gaelicization of the elite, rather than as the conquest of Cináed mac Ailpín. Woolf also argues that the Pictish kingdom of Fortriu was in Moray, north of the Grampian mountains, and not in Strathearn.

fuentes/from-pictland-to-alba-woolf/por_.texto: It is the reference synthesis for the period; his location of Fortriu has been accepted by many, and his account of Gaelicization remains under discussion.

fuentes/pagan-celtic-ireland-raftery/tit.texto: Pagan Celtic Ireland: The Enigma of the Irish Iron Age

fuentes/pagan-celtic-ireland-raftery/res.texto: Synthesis of Irish Iron Age archaeology: La Tène objects from the north and centre of the island, royal sites (Emain Macha, Dún Ailinne, Tara), trackways such as the one at Corlea, large earthworks, and bog bodies. Raftery points out how little is known about settlements and daily life, and that nothing proves a Celtic invasion.

fuentes/pagan-celtic-ireland-raftery/por.texto: It was the reference work until the studies of the 2010s; its title, which calls pagan Ireland “Celtic,” reflects a habit that Raftery's own evidence called into question.

fuentes/navan-fort-lynn/resumen.texto: Lynn publishes and discusses the excavations at Emain Macha: the sequence of houses from the Late Bronze Age and Iron Age, the great 40-metre structure with its central post of around 95 BC and its ritual destruction, and the relationship between the royal site and the Emain Macha of the sagas.

fuentes/navan-fort-lynn/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main study of the site. Lynn avoids reading the archaeology through the medieval sagas, although he acknowledges that its memory as a special place survived.

fuentes/a-guide-to-ogam-mcmanus/resumen.texto: Study of the ogham alphabet and its inscriptions: the system of strokes and the names of the letters (after trees, according to the later tradition), the language of the stones and its evolution, the relation to Latin grammar, and the scholarly tradition of ogham in medieval manuscripts. McManus argues that ogham was created in Ireland, probably in the 4th century, by someone who knew the Latin classification of letters.

fuentes/a-guide-to-ogam-mcmanus/por_que_.texto: It is the reference work on ogham; its proposed date rests on linguistics, because no stone is securely dated by other means.

fuentes/a-guide-to-early-irish-law-kelly.texto: A Guide to Early Irish Law

Handbook that sets out the content of the Irish legal treatises of the 7th and 8th centuries: social grades, the king and the kingdom, women, the family, marriage and divorce, clientship, contracts, offences and penalties (compensatory payments rather than corporal punishment), jurists and procedures.
It is the standard introduction to the law of early medieval Ireland; Kelly stresses the ecclesiastical influence on the texts and the possible distance between the treatises and practice.

fuentes/irish-kings-and-high-kings-byrne.texto: History of Irish kingship in the early Middle Ages, kingdom by kingdom, which shows that the idea of a “high king of Ireland” seated at Tara was a claim of the Uí Néill, elaborated by their scholars between the 7th and 9th centuries, and not a real national monarchy until Brian Boru and his successors.
It fixed the current view of Irish kingship; later research (Charles-Edwards, Jaski) qualified how much the kingship of Tara weighed before the 9th century.

fuentes/the-church-in-early-irish-societ.texto: The Church in Early Irish Society

Hughes argued that the Irish Church began with bishops and dioceses, as in Britain and Gaul, and that in the 7th century it was displaced by large federations of monasteries (paruchiae) led by abbots, adapted to a society without cities.
It was the dominant model for twenty years. Richard Sharpe (1984) and Colmán Etchingham questioned it: bishops remained important, and the “monastic Church” is partly an illusion of the sources.

fuentes/iglesia-irlandesa-sharpe-1984/ti.texto: Some Problems Concerning the Organization of the Church in Early Medieval Ireland

fuentes/iglesia-irlandesa-sharpe-1984/re.texto: Sharpe argues that there was no shift from an episcopal Church to a monastic one: Irish churches always combined bishops, abbots and communities of different sizes, and the legal texts show a network of local churches with pastoral functions.

fuentes/iglesia-irlandesa-sharpe-1984/po.texto: Together with Etchingham's work, it dismantled the image of a monastic “Celtic Church” distinct from Rome, an image that had also been used for confessional purposes; some historians believe he underestimates the distinctive power of Irish abbots.

fuentes/early-christian-ireland-charles-.texto: History of Ireland from the arrival of Christianity to the end of the 8th century: the conversion, Palladius and Patrick, society and kingship, the Church and the monasteries, the Easter controversy and relations with the Britons, the Picts and the Angles.
It is the reference synthesis for the period, with a close reading of the sources; its density and its focus on institutions rather than social life are noted as limitations.

fuentes/studies-in-irish-literature-and-.texto: Studies in Irish Literature and History

Collection of essays in which Carney, against the idea of a pagan oral tradition copied as it was, argues that Irish sagas are works of learned monastic authors, influenced by Latin and Christian literature, and that they must be read as written literature. He discusses, among other things, the Voyage of Brendan, the story of Tristan and the biography of Patrick.

It founded the critical current that McCone and others later developed; many of his specific proposals about Latin sources were not accepted, and he was criticized for pushing the denial of oral tradition to an extreme.

fuentes/pagan-past-and-christian-present.texto: Pagan Past and Christian Present in Early Irish Literature

McCone argues that early Irish literature, sagas included, is the work of monastic scholars who knew the Bible, the Church Fathers and Latin literature, and that they wrote it for their own time; themes that the “nativists” read as pagan survivals (sacred kingship, the hero, the women of the otherworld) are better explained by biblical models and by Church ideology.

It is the central book of the “anti-nativist” current, which changed the study of Irish literature against Jackson's idea of a “window on the Iron Age.” Its critics, such as Proinsias Mac Cana, accept monastic authorship but reproach it for underestimating the traditional elements that the monks reworked.

fuentes/in-search-of-the-irish-dreamtime.texto: In Search of the Irish Dreamtime: Archaeology and Early Irish Literature

Mallory compares what the Irish sagas describe (chariots, weapons, houses, feasts, royal sites) with what the archaeology of the Iron Age and the Early Middle Ages shows, and concludes that almost all of it corresponds to Ireland of the 7th to 10th centuries, the time of the authors, and not to the Iron Age.

It takes up the debate between Jackson and McCone with archaeological data and tilts it toward McCone; it nonetheless acknowledges some isolated ancient elements, such as the chariots or the memory of certain royal sites.

fuentes/the-age-of-conquest-davies/resum.texto: History of Wales from the death of Gruffudd ap Llywelyn to the rebellion of Owain Glyndŵr: the Norman conquest of the marches, the rise of the princes of Gwynedd, the conquest by Edward I, and Welsh society under English rule. Davies analyzes the conquest as a colonial process and Welsh identity as a response to it.

fuentes/the-age-of-conquest-davies/por_q.texto: It is the standard reference on medieval Wales, reissued in 1991 as The Age of Conquest; some English historians criticized it for reading English expansion through modern colonial categories.

fuentes/lapida-de-distancia-de-bridgenes.texto: Sandstone slab with inscription and reliefs

Slab that Legio II Augusta dedicated to Antoninus Pius on completing its section of the Antonine Wall: the central inscription states that the legion completed 4,652 paces. The side panels show a Roman horseman and four naked Britons (one trampled, another fleeing with a spear in his back, another seated and another bound and beheaded), and the sacrifice of a bull, a pig and a ram (suovetaurilia) before the work. It is the best preserved of the distance slabs that the legions set up along the wall; it was found in 1868 and is held by the National Museum of Scotland.
It is a contemporary document about the northern frontier in 142, and it shows how Roman builders depicted the inhabitants of present-day Scotland: a propaganda image, not a portrait.
Inscription and description in Roman Inscriptions of Britain (RIB 2139)

fuentes/panegirico-anonimo-a-constantino.texto: Speech delivered at the court of Constantine in Trier in 310. Reviewing the life of his father Constantius, it says that his last expedition did not seek “British trophies”, as was believed, but reached the limit of the lands, and that he had no interest in “the forests and marshes of the Caledonians and other Picts”, nor in Hibernia or Thule. It is the only contemporary mention of Caledonia linked to the campaign of 305-306, and it is rhetorical: it gives no itinerary or results.
It documents that, at the start of the 4th century, Rome was again operating in the north of Britain, and it shows how the Picts were spoken of from the court.
Latin text on Wikisource (chapter VII deals with Constantius’s last expedition)

personas/casivelauno/resumen.texto: British chieftain to whom, according to Caesar (BG V.11-22), the tribes of the southeast gave command against the second Roman expedition of 54 BC. Caesar says that he dismissed his infantry and harassed the Romans with some 4000 war chariots, that he lost his stronghold north of the Thames (which Wheeler placed at Wheathampstead, an identification that is not certain), and that he surrendered through Comius, handed over hostages and accepted a tribute. We know him only from Caesar and from authors who follow him (Cassius Dio, Orosius); his real power over the other tribes and the tribute, which nothing indicates was ever paid, depend on the victor's account.

personas/mandubracio/resumen.texto: Young Trinovantian noble whose father had been killed by Cassivellaunus, according to Caesar (BG V.20); he took refuge in Gaul with Caesar and returned with him in 54 BC. The Trinovantes asked that he be placed at the head of their people, and Roman protection of him was one of the conditions of Cassivellaunus's surrender.

personas/dubnovelauno/resumen.texto: British king known from coins bearing the legend DVBNOVELLAVNOS, minted in Essex and Kent toward the end of the 1st century BC. Augustus names him in his Res Gestae (32) among the kings who took refuge with him as suppliants, so it is supposed that a rival drove him out, perhaps from the Catuvellauni.

personas/tincomaro/resumen.texto: King of the Atrebates of southern Britain, who on his coins is called son of Comius (COM F) and whose pieces imitate Roman models. Augustus names him in his Res Gestae (32) as a British king who took refuge with him, around the year 7; it is believed that his brother Epillus displaced him.

personas/epilo/resumen.texto: King of the Atrebates known only from his coins, which are said to be those of a son of Comius and bear the legends REX and CALLEV: they are among the first in Britain to use the Latin title of king and to name a place, Calleva (Silchester). Later his coins appear in Kent.

personas/verica/resumen.texto: King of the Atrebates whose coins bear VERICA REX and Roman motifs, such as the vine leaf, a sign of a client kingdom of Rome. Around 41-42 he was expelled, probably by the Catuvellauni, and took refuge in Rome: Cassius Dio (LX.19) tells that a certain Bericus convinced Claudius to invade the island, and most historians identify him with that man.

personas/tasciovano/resumen.texto: King of the Catuvellauni known only from his coins, minted mostly at Verulamium (with the mark VER) and sometimes with the title RICON, a British word meaning “king.” Cunobelinus and others present themselves on his coins as his sons.

personas/cunobelino/resumen.texto: The most powerful British king before the conquest: from Camulodunum (Colchester) he dominated the Catuvellauni and the Trinovantes and minted large quantities of gold with the barley ear and the legends CVNOBELINVS REX and CAMV. Suetonius (Caligula 44) calls him “king of the Britons,” and Roman imports from his lands show trade with Roman Gaul. He died shortly before the invasion of 43; Shakespeare turned him into the Cymbeline of his play.

personas/adminio/resumen.texto: Son of Cunobelinus, expelled by his father, who surrendered to Caligula around 40 with a few followers, according to Suetonius (Caligula 44); the emperor presented it to Rome as if the whole island had surrendered. His coins, bearing the legend AMMINIVS, appear in Kent.

personas/togodumno/resumen.texto: Son of Cunobelinus who led, together with his brother Caratacus, the resistance against the invasion of Claudius. Cassius Dio (LX.20-21) tells that he was defeated by Aulus Plautius and died shortly after the battles of the Medway and the Thames; some historians (Hind) propose that he survived and is the same person as Togidubnus, a hypothesis most do not accept.

personas/carataco/resumen.texto: Son of Cunobelinus who, after the defeat of 43, continued the war for eight years at the head of the Silures and Ordovices of what is now Wales, according to Tacitus (Annals XII.33-38). Defeated by Ostorius Scapula around 51, he took refuge with the queen of the Brigantes, Cartimandua, who handed him over in chains to the Romans. Taken to Rome with his family, Tacitus puts a speech before Claudius in his mouth and tells that the emperor pardoned him; Cassius Dio attributes to him the question of why the Romans, with all they had, coveted the poor tents of the Britons. Both speeches are compositions by the historians, not recorded words. His figure entered English theater with Caratach in John Fletcher's Bonduca (around 1613), and in the 18th and 19th centuries he became a national hero of both Wales and England.

personas/cartimandua/resumen.texto: Queen of the Brigantes of northern Britain, allied with Rome from the first years of the conquest; Tacitus (Annals XII.36 and 40; Histories III.45) is almost the only source. She handed Caratacus over to the Romans in 51, which according to Tacitus brought her wealth and power. She separated from her husband Venutius and married her armor-bearer Velocatus, which provoked civil wars among the Brigantes; in 69 Venutius rose up and the Romans could only rescue her. Tacitus presents her with contempt, as a lustful and treacherous queen; she is the only British queen we know of who ruled in her own right, and everything we know about her comes through an author who considers it dishonorable for the Brigantes to be “under the command of a woman” (Annals XII.40).

personas/venucio/resumen.texto: Husband of Cartimandua and Brigantian chief, whom Tacitus (Annals XII.40) calls, after the capture of Caratacus, the most skilled Briton in war; he was an ally of Rome while he was married to the queen. He broke with his wife and with Rome and attacked her in the time of governor Didius Gallus (52-57), and in 69 (Histories III.45), taking advantage of the Roman civil war, drove her out of the kingdom; the campaigns of Petillius Cerialis (71-74) ended his resistance, although the sources do not say what became of him.

personas/prasutago/resumen.texto: King of the Iceni, an ally of Rome, known from Tacitus (Annals XIV.31). On his death he left his kingdom as an inheritance to the emperor Nero and his two daughters, to protect it; Roman officials treated it as booty, and that set off the revolt of his widow, Boudica. Coins bearing the legend SVB RII PRASTO are attributed to him, a reading that is debated.

personas/boudica/resumen.texto: Widow of Prasutagus and queen of the Iceni who led, in 60 or 61, the largest rebellion against Rome in Britain. According to Tacitus (Annals XIV.31-37; Agricola 16), the Romans flogged her and raped her daughters when they annexed the kingdom; together with the Trinovantes she destroyed Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium and was defeated by Suetonius Paulinus in a battle in a place now unknown. Cassius Dio (LXII.1-12), who wrote a century and a half later and reaches us summarized by Xiphilinus, describes her as tall, with a harsh voice and red hair down to her waist, wearing a large gold torc; he attributes to her a long speech and cruelties against Roman women. Tacitus says that she poisoned herself, Dio that she fell ill and died. The death tolls given by both (70,000 and 80,000) are probable exaggerations; her image as a national heroine was born in Elizabethan and Victorian England.

personas/togidubno/resumen.texto: Client king of southern Britain, probably of the regni or the Atrebates, to whom according to Tacitus (Agricola 14) Rome entrusted several tribes, and who remained loyal “to our own day.” An inscription from Chichester (RIB 91) names him Tiberius Claudius [...]gidubnus, with Roman citizenship received from Claudius; the first letters were lost, and the form Togidubnus is a restoration (the manuscripts of Tacitus give Cogidumnus and Togidumnus), as is his title, which was once read as “king and legate of Augustus” and is now read as “great king of Britain.” The palace at Fishbourne is often attributed to him, an attribution with no direct proof.

personas/aulo-placio/resumen.texto: Roman senator who led the invasion of Britain in 43, according to Cassius Dio (LX.19-21), and was its first governor until 47. His army had four legions (II Augusta, IX Hispana, XIV and XX), a number that Dio does not give but that is deduced from inscriptions and from Tacitus. He defeated Caratacus and Togodumnus at the Medway and waited for Claudius before taking Camulodunum; on his return to Rome he received an ovation, with the emperor walking at his side (Dio LX.30; Suetonius, Claudius 24).

personas/publio-ostorio-escapula/resumen.texto: Second governor of Britain (47-52). According to Tacitus (Annals XII.31-39), he disarmed the allied tribes, which provoked the uprising of the Iceni in 47, founded the veterans' colony of Camulodunum, and defeated Caratacus around 51; he died in office, exhausted by the guerrilla warfare of the Silures.

personas/cayo-suetonio-paulino/resumen.texto: Roman general who, according to Pliny (Natural History V.14), was the first Roman general to cross the Atlas Mountains, in Mauretania, and governor of Britain from 58 to 61. He attacked the island of Mona (Anglesey), refuge of fugitives and druids, and while he was there the revolt of Boudica broke out, which he defeated; Tacitus (Annals XIV.29-39) tells that his later harshness led Rome to replace him.

personas/cato-deciano/resumen.texto: Financial procurator of Britain in 60. Tacitus (Annals XIV.32) blames his greed for the revolt of Boudica and tells that, when the attack came, he sent only 200 men to Camulodunum and fled to Gaul; Cassius Dio (LXII.2) adds that he demanded the return of the subsidies that Claudius had given to the British chiefs.

personas/julio-clasiciano/resumen.texto: Procurator of Britain appointed after the revolt of Boudica, of Gaulish family; according to Tacitus (Annals XIV.38) he informed Rome that the war would not end while Suetonius Paulinus remained, which led to his replacement. His tombstone, found in London in 1852 and 1935 (RIB 12), was set up by his wife, Julia Pacata, daughter of a Treveran nobleman.

personas/quinto-petilio-cerial/resumen.texto: Legate of Legion IX Hispana who in 60 marched against Boudica and lost almost all his infantry, according to Tacitus (Annals XIV.32). After suppressing the Batavian revolt in 70, he governed Britain (71-74) and defeated the Brigantes of Venutius; from his time dates the legionary fortress of York.

personas/cneo-julio-agricola/resumen.texto: Governor of Britain between 77 or 78 and 84, who conquered north Wales, advanced into northern Scotland and defeated the Caledonians at Mons Graupius. We know him mainly through the biography written by his son-in-law Tacitus, a eulogy that credits him with the whole conquest and criticizes Domitian for recalling him to Rome. According to Tacitus (Agricola 24) he believed Ireland could be taken with one legion, and his fleet sailed around Britain.
