personas/calgaco/resumen.texto: Chief of the Caledonians at the battle of Mons Graupius, the first inhabitant of Scotland whose name is known, and known only from Tacitus (Agricola 29-32). Tacitus attributes to him a speech against Roman imperialism that ends with the phrase “where they make a desert, they call it peace” (ubi solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant). The speech is a rhetorical composition by Tacitus, who uses it to criticize Rome through a barbarian; some doubt that Calgacus (“the one with the sword”) existed at all.

personas/septimio-severo/resumen.texto: Roman emperor born in Leptis Magna who in 208 led a large expedition to Britain against the Caledonians and the Maeatae, with his sons Caracalla and Geta. Cassius Dio (LXXVI.11-15 in Boissevain's numbering; LXXVII in the Loeb edition) and Herodian (III.14-15) recount the campaign, in which, according to Dio, Rome lost 50,000 men to guerrilla warfare and the terrain, a figure that cannot be verified. He died in York in 211.

personas/argentocoxos/resumen.texto: Caledonian chief whose name means “silver leg,” known only from an anecdote told by Cassius Dio (LXXVI.16.5 in Boissevain's numbering; LXXVII.16.5 in the Loeb edition), set after the peace agreements of around 210: his wife, whom the empress Julia Domna reproached for the sexual freedom of Caledonian women, replied that they openly united with the best men, while Roman women let themselves be seduced in secret by the worst. The scene repeats the Greek and Roman commonplace that sets barbarian virtue against Roman corruption, and it is the only time a Caledonian woman speaks in the sources, although Dio does not give her name.

personas/magno-maximo/resumen.texto: Spanish general in command of the army of Britain, who in 383 proclaimed himself emperor, defeated Gratian and governed Gaul, Hispania and Britain from Trier until Theodosius defeated him and had him killed in 388. Gildas blames him for leaving the island without soldiers; Welsh tradition turned him into Macsen Wledig, ancestor of dynasties (named on the Pillar of Eliseg) and protagonist of a story in the Mabinogion.

personas/constantino-iii/resumen.texto: Soldier proclaimed emperor by the army of Britain in 407, who crossed to Gaul with the island's troops and ruled from Arles until he was defeated and executed in 411. His usurpation left Britain without a garrison; according to Zosimus (VI.5), in 409 the Britons expelled their officials and governed themselves.

personas/pelagio/resumen.texto: Monk and theologian born in Britain, who taught in Rome that human beings can do good through their free will without depending on grace. Augustine of Hippo and Jerome fought him (Jerome mocks him as a man “loaded with Scottish porridge”), and the Church condemned him in 418. Prosper of Aquitaine and Constantius of Lyon tell that his ideas had followers in Britain.

personas/german-de-auxerre/resumen.texto: Bishop of Auxerre who in 429, according to the chronicle of Prosper and the life written by Constantius of Lyon around 480, was sent to Britain with Lupus of Troyes to combat the followers of Pelagius. Constantius tells that he debated them in public, that he visited the tomb of St Alban and that he led the Britons to a bloodless victory against Picts and Saxons with the cry of “Alleluia.” He is one of the few contemporary witnesses to post-Roman Britain, although it is written as a saint's life.

personas/vortigern/resumen.texto: British ruler of the 5th century, whom tradition blames for inviting the Saxons as mercenaries against the Picts and Scots. Gildas speaks only of a “proud tyrant” (some manuscripts add the name), Bede calls him Vurtigernus, and the Historia Brittonum devotes a novelistic story to him with Hengist and Horsa; the 9th-century Pillar of Eliseg makes him an ancestor of the kings of Powys. The name means “great lord,” and it is debated whether it is a personal name or a title.

personas/ambrosio-aureliano/resumen.texto: British chief of the second half of the 5th century who, according to Gildas (De excidio 25), gathered the survivors and defeated the Saxons. Gildas describes him as a moderate man, perhaps the only one of Roman lineage to survive the catastrophe, in which his parents died, who “certainly wore the purple” (a phrase debated as an allusion to imperial or consular rank). He is the only figure of British resistance named by an author who was almost a contemporary; the Historia Brittonum turns him into a prophet child, Emrys, and Geoffrey of Monmouth into the uncle of Arthur.

personas/arturo/resumen.texto: British military leader who would have fought the Saxons around 500, whose historical existence is disputed. Gildas and Bede do not name him; he first appears in a verse of the Gododdin, perhaps interpolated, in the Historia Brittonum (c. 829), which credits him with twelve battles, and in the Annales Cambriae (10th century), which date Badon to 516 and his death at Camlann to 537. Historians such as Alcock (1971) and John Morris (1973) accepted him as a real chief; Dumville (1977) argued that there is no historical evidence for him, Padel (1994) that he was born as a figure of folklore and historicized later, and Halsall (2013) that the sources do not allow us to know whether he existed. Among academic historians this skeptical or agnostic position predominates today; the king of legend is the work of Geoffrey of Monmouth (1136) and of later literature.

personas/riotamo/resumen.texto: “King of the Britons” who, according to Jordanes (Getica 237-238), arrived by sea with 12,000 men around 469 to help the emperor Anthemius against the Visigoths, and was defeated by Euric at Déols, after which he fled to the Burgundians. Sidonius Apollinaris wrote him a letter (III.9). It is evidence that there were Britons with military strength in Gaul; its identification with Arthur, proposed by Geoffrey Ashe in 1985, has no support in the sources.

personas/gildas/resumen.texto: British monk of the 6th century, author of De excidio Britanniae, the only surviving text written in Britain by a Briton of that period. He says he was born in the year of the battle of Mount Badon, in an ambiguous passage that is usually read as meaning that he was writing forty-three or forty-four years later; he condemns five British kings and the clergy for their sins, which in his view explain the Saxon conquest. The date of the work is debated: the most accepted is around 530-545 (Maelgwn, one of the kings he condemns, died around 547), but Higham and others move it to the late 5th century. Lives written in the 11th and 12th centuries have him die in Brittany, at Rhuys; the Annales Cambriae and the Irish annals date his death around 570.

personas/maelgwn-gwynedd/resumen.texto: King of Gwynedd, the most powerful of the five kings whom Gildas condemns under the name Maglocunus, “dragon of the island,” and whom he accuses of killing his uncle and his nephew and of abandoning monastic life. According to the Annales Cambriae he died in a “great mortality” in 547, which is usually identified with the plague of Justinian.

personas/vortiporio/resumen.texto: King of the Demetae (Dyfed), whom Gildas condemns as a “tyrant,” the son of a good king. A stone from Castell Dwyran, in Carmarthenshire, bears in Latin MEMORIA VOTEPORIGIS PROTICTORIS and in ogham VOTECORIGAS: if it is him, as many believe, he is one of the few kings of the period with a monument of his own, and it shows the mixture of Roman and Irish tradition in Dyfed.

personas/sanson-de-dol/resumen.texto: Monk born in south Wales, a disciple of Iltud, who passed through Cornwall and founded the monastery of Dol in Armorica. His Latin life, the oldest of any British saint, is dated between the 7th and 9th centuries; a “Samson peccator episcopus” signs the acts of a council of Paris held between 556 and 573, which confirms his existence and his role in the British emigration.

personas/david-de-gales/resumen.texto: Bishop and founder of the monastery of Mynyw (St Davids), patron saint of Wales. Almost everything told about him comes from the life written by Rhygyfarch around 1095, five centuries later, to defend the independence of his see against Canterbury; the annals mention him only briefly.

personas/ninian/resumen.texto: British bishop who, according to Bede (Ecclesiastical History III.4), converted the southern Picts and founded a stone church at Whithorn called Candida Casa. Bede writes centuries later and gives the report as tradition; the date is uncertain, and Thomas Clancy (2001) proposed that “Ninian” is a copying error for Uinniau, the Irish saint Finnian, a hypothesis that is debated.

personas/taliesin/resumen.texto: Sixth-century British poet whom the Historia Brittonum (ch. 62) names among the famous bards of his time. About a dozen poems of the Book of Taliesin, which praise Urien of Rheged, his son Owain and Cynan Garwyn of Powys, have been considered possibly authentic since the studies of Ifor Williams; the rest of the book is later, and medieval legend made him a magical seer.

personas/aneirin/resumen.texto: British poet to whom tradition attributes the Gododdin, the lament for the warriors of Din Eidyn who died at Catraeth around 600. The Historia Brittonum names him alongside Taliesin; nothing certain is known of his life, and whether a single poet wrote a text that grew for centuries is debated.

personas/urien-de-rheged/resumen.texto: King of Rheged, in northern Britain, celebrated in the poems of Taliesin as a warrior and a generous lord. According to the Historia Brittonum (ch. 63) he led a British coalition that besieged the Angles at Lindisfarne, and he was murdered out of envy, at the instigation of another British king, Morcant.

personas/rhydderch-hael/resumen.texto: King of Alt Clut (Dumbarton), the British kingdom of the Clyde; he appears in Adomnán's Life of Columba (I.15), which calls him “Roderc, son of Tóthal, who reigned on the rock of the Clyde,” and in the Historia Brittonum alongside Urien. He is one of the best documented northern British kings of the 6th century.

personas/cadwallon-ap-cadfan/resumen.texto: King of Gwynedd who, allied with the pagan king Penda of Mercia, defeated and killed Edwin of Northumbria at Hatfield Chase in 633 and devastated his kingdom, until Oswald killed him in 634. Bede (II.20, III.1) presents him as a Christian tyrant worse than a pagan; Welsh tradition presents him as a hero who came close to recovering the island.

personas/paladio/resumen.texto: Deacon, probably Gaulish, whom Pope Celestine sent in 431 as the first bishop “to the Scots who believe in Christ,” according to the chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine: the oldest and most secure date for Christianity in Ireland, which proves there were Christians before Patrick. It is not known how much he worked on the island; later tradition overshadowed him with Patrick and attributed part of his story to him.

personas/loegaire-mac-neill/resumen.texto: King of Tara in the 5th century, son of Niall according to the genealogies, whom Muirchú's life of Patrick sets against the saint at the Easter fire of Slane and Tara. Tírechán tells that he was buried standing and armed, facing his enemies in Leinster, a sign that tradition remembered him as a pagan.

personas/niall-noigiallach/resumen.texto: Semi-legendary king of Tara, eponymous ancestor of the Uí Néill, the dynasty that dominated northern and central Ireland for six centuries. The annals give him contradictory dates at the end of the 4th or the beginning of the 5th century, and the sagas have him raid Britain and Gaul; nothing of his life is documented by contemporary sources. A 2006 genetic study (Moore and others) linked a Y-chromosome lineage very common in northwest Ireland with the Uí Néill, but attributing it to Niall is a conjecture.

personas/brigida-de-kildare/resumen.texto: Founder of the double monastery of Kildare and one of the three patron saints of Ireland. The oldest life, by Cogitosus (around 650-680), is made of miracles and gives no firm biographical data; the annals date her death to around 524-526. Her name is that of an Irish goddess, and since the 19th century it has been debated how much of that cult passed to the saint (that debate belongs to the Celtic religion package).

personas/cogitoso/resumen.texto: Monk of Kildare who wrote, around 650-680, the Latin life of Brigid, the oldest surviving Irish hagiography. In it he claims for Kildare primacy over almost all the churches of Ireland and describes the monastery's great wooden church.

personas/ciaran-de-clonmacnoise/resumen.texto: Founder of the monastery of Clonmacnoise, on the banks of the Shannon, around 544-545, where he died young, according to the annals, in the plague of 549. The monastery was one of the great centers of the Church and of writing in Irish; the Lebor na hUidre was copied there.

personas/brendan-de-clonfert/resumen.texto: Irish abbot of the 6th century, founder of Clonfert, famous for the Voyage of St Brendan, a Latin tale written two or three centuries later about his voyage across the ocean in search of the “promised land of the saints.” His real journeys to Scotland and perhaps Brittany are possible; the idea that he reached America has no support in the sources.

personas/kevin-de-glendalough/resumen.texto: Hermit and founder of the monastery of Glendalough, in the Wicklow Mountains; the annals date his death to 618, and tradition gives him a life of one hundred and twenty years. His lives, which are late, are full of animal stories and asceticism.

personas/diarmait-mac-cerbaill/resumen.texto: King of Tara in the 6th century, the last one who, according to the Annals of Ulster, celebrated the “feast of Tara” (feis Temro), in 560, an inauguration rite that has been interpreted as pagan. Later tradition set him against Columba and against the saint Ruadán, to whom the “curse” that left Tara deserted was attributed; those stories are centuries later.

personas/aidan-de-lindisfarne/resumen.texto: Monk of Iona whom King Oswald brought to Northumbria in 635 to convert the English; he founded Lindisfarne and was its bishop until his death in 651. Bede (III.3-17), although he did not share his way of calculating Easter, describes him with admiration for his poverty and for his preaching on foot.

personas/adomnan/resumen.texto: Ninth abbot of Iona (679-704), a distant relative of Columba. He wrote the Life of Columba and De locis sanctis, on the holy places, and at the synod of Birr in 697 he promulgated the Cáin Adomnáin, a law that protected women, children and clerics in war. He tried to get Iona to accept the Roman Easter, without succeeding in his lifetime.

personas/muirchu/resumen.texto: Cleric of Leinster who wrote, around 680-700, a life of Patrick preserved in the Book of Armagh, dedicated to Bishop Áed of Sleaty. He is the source of the legendary Patrick: the challenge of the Easter fire at Slane before King Loegaire and the contests with the druids, stories that serve Armagh's claim to lead the Irish Church.

personas/aedan-mac-gabrain/resumen.texto: King of Dál Riata, the Gaelic kingdom of Argyll, from around 574. Adomnán tells that Columba ordained him king, the first consecration of a king recorded in Britain and Ireland; he campaigned in Orkney, on the Isle of Man and against the Picts, and Bede (I.34) says that Æthelfrith of Northumbria defeated him at Degsastan in 603.

personas/bridei-mac-maelchon/resumen.texto: King of the Picts, the first one of whom anything certain is known. Adomnán (II.33-35) tells that Columba visited him at his fortress near the River Ness, and Bede (III.4) that Columba converted the northern Picts during his reign; the Annals of Ulster record his victory over the Gaels of Dál Riata in 558 or 560 and his death around 584.

personas/bridei-mac-bili/resumen.texto: King of Fortriu, the dominant Pictish kingdom, who in 685 defeated and killed King Ecgfrith of Northumbria at Dún Nechtain and ended Anglian domination over the Picts. His father was a British king of Alt Clut, an example of the ties between the dynasties of the north.

personas/nechtan-mac-der-ilei/resumen.texto: King of the Picts who around 710-715 asked for advice from Abbot Ceolfrith of Wearmouth-Jarrow and adopted the Roman Easter and tonsure, according to Bede (V.21). According to the Annals of Ulster, in 717 he expelled the clergy of Iona “beyond the spine of Britain”; he abdicated, became a monk and later fought to regain the throne.

personas/oengus-mac-fergusa/resumen.texto: King of the Picts who between 736 and 741, according to the Annals of Ulster, took Dunadd and subjected Dál Riata, and who campaigned against the Britons of Alt Clut and against Northumbria. A continuator of Bede calls him a “bloody tyrant”; he was the most powerful king of northern Britain of his time.

personas/cinaed-mac-ailpin/resumen.texto: King whom Scottish tradition considers the unifier of Picts and Scots and the first king of Scotland, around 843. The Annals of Ulster, recording his death in 858, call him “king of the Picts”; the story of a Gaelic conquest of the Picts and the “treachery of MacAlpin” comes from later chronicles, and present-day historians (Woolf, Broun) see a longer process of Gaelicization.

personas/rhodri-mawr/resumen.texto: King of Gwynedd who added Powys and Seisyllwg and ruled much of Wales. The Annals of Ulster record that in 856 he killed Horm, chief of the Danish Vikings; the Annales Cambriae say that the English killed him in 878.

personas/hywel-dda/resumen.texto: King of Deheubarth who came to rule almost all of Wales, accepted the overlordship of the English king Athelstan, and made a pilgrimage to Rome in 928; he is the only Welsh king whose own coinage is known. Tradition credits him with codifying Welsh law at an assembly in Whitland, but the manuscripts of those laws date from the 13th and 14th centuries, and their relationship to him is debated.

personas/gruffudd-ap-llywelyn/resumen.texto: King of Gwynedd and, from around 1055, of all of Wales, the only ruler to govern the whole Welsh territory. He attacked the English border with success until Harold Godwinson's campaign of 1063 cornered him, and his own men killed him and sent his head to Harold.

personas/llywelyn-ab-iorwerth/resumen.texto: Prince of Gwynedd, called the Great, who came to dominate almost all of Wales; he married Joan, daughter of King John of England, and allied himself with the rebel barons of Magna Carta, who recognized his rights. He organized his principality with officials and a chancery in the manner of the neighboring kingdoms.

personas/llywelyn-ap-gruffudd/resumen.texto: Grandson of Llywelyn the Great and the only Welsh prince recognized by the English crown as Prince of Wales, in the Treaty of Montgomery of 1267. He lost the war of 1277 against Edward I, rose up again in 1282 and died in an ambush near Cilmeri on 11 December that year; his head was displayed in the Tower of London. Welsh tradition calls him Llywelyn Ein Llyw Olaf, “our last leader.”

personas/dafydd-ap-gruffudd/resumen.texto: Brother of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, who alternated between alliance with the English and rebellion, and whose uprising of 1282 began the last war. After his brother's death the resistance went on for a few months; captured in 1283, Edward I had him hanged, disemboweled and quartered at Shrewsbury for treason.

personas/giraldo-cambrense/resumen.texto: Cleric of Norman and Welsh family (Gerald de Barri) who accompanied Prince John to Ireland in 1185 and Archbishop Baldwin through Wales in 1188. He wrote the Topography of Ireland, the Conquest of Ireland, the Itinerary and the Description of Wales: these are the main sources on the Norman conquest and on how a 12th-century cleric saw the Irish and the Welsh, mixing direct observation, prejudice and propaganda.

personas/diarmait-mac-murchada/resumen.texto: King of Leinster who, deposed in 1166 by the high king Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair and by Tigernán Ua Ruairc (whose wife he had abducted in 1152), asked Henry II of England for help and recruited Anglo-Norman knights from Wales. With them he recovered his kingdom from 1169 and married his daughter Aífe to Strongbow, whom he made his heir; he died at Ferns in 1171. Nationalist historiography called him a traitor; his motivation, according to most historians, was to recover his kingdom, not to hand Ireland over.

personas/strongbow/resumen.texto: Earl of Pembroke called Strongbow, who landed in Ireland in 1170, took Waterford and Dublin, and married Aífe, daughter of Diarmait Mac Murchada, so inheriting Leinster in 1171. His power led Henry II to go to Ireland in person in 1171 to impose his authority.

personas/ruaidri-ua-conchobair/resumen.texto: King of Connacht and, from 1166, high king of Ireland, the last one recognized as such. He could not drive out the Anglo-Normans, and in the Treaty of Windsor of 1175 he accepted the sovereignty of Henry II in exchange for ruling the lands not in Norman hands; he died in retirement at the monastery of Cong.

personas/aulo-didio-galo/resumen.texto: Roman senator, suffect consul in 39 and proconsul of Asia, who governed Britain from 52 to 57, from the death in office of Ostorius Scapula, while Wales, above all the Silures, kept resisting. According to Tacitus (Agricola 14; Annals XII.40) he was content to keep what had been won and push forward a few forts; Sheppard Frere thinks he was following Claudius’s instructions, since Claudius saw no advantage in conquering difficult terrain. He sent troops to aid the Brigantian queen Cartimandua against the first uprising of Venutius.

personas/quinto-veranio/resumen.texto: Governor of the province of Lycia (43–48), consul in 49 and governor of Britain from 57, where he changed his predecessor’s policy and began operations against the Silures of Wales. He died in office in 57 or 58. Tacitus (Agricola 14) says he died before completing a year in office; and in his will, which Tacitus records (Annals XIV.29), he flattered Nero and assured him that with two more years he would have subdued the province (“subiecturum ei provinciam”). The speed with which his successor Suetonius Paulinus advanced in Wales suggests that Veranius had already done much of the work. Onasander dedicated his treatise on strategy to him.

personas/marco-trebelio-maximo/resumen.texto: Suffect consul in 55 with Seneca and governor of Britain from 63 to 69. He pursued a policy of consolidation without conquering new territory, and refounded Camulodunum after Boudica’s revolt. According to Tacitus, the idle troops mutinied; Trebellius went into hiding and then governed only through the tolerance of the soldiers (Agricola 16). In 69, hated for his greed and accused by Roscius Caelius, legate of Legio XX Valeria Victrix, of impoverishing the legions, he fled to Vitellius (Histories I.60); Vitellius appointed Vettius Bolanus in his place (Histories II.65). A lead ingot found in Wrexham in 2019 bears his name; it is the only inscription from Britain that mentions him.

personas/sexto-julio-frontino/resumen.texto: Consul three times and governor of Britain from a few years after 70, successor to Petillius Cerialis and predecessor of Agricola (77). According to Tacitus (Agricola 17) he subdued the Silures of southern Wales, and it is believed that he also fought the Brigantes; the fort at Cardiff dates from his time. He was proconsul of Asia around 86, and in 97 Nerva appointed him curator aquarum of Rome, a post from which came his report on the aqueducts, De aquaeductu; he also wrote a treatise on military stratagems. He died in 103 or 104.

personas/owain-ap-hywel-dda/resumen.texto: Son of Hywel Dda. When Hywel died in 950 (949 or 950, depending on the source), the kingdom was divided among his brothers according to Welsh law; from 954 he ruled Deheubarth alone, in southern Wales. He could not keep hegemony over Gwynedd, which the sons of Idwal Foel recovered; in 962 he promised an annual tribute to the English king Edgar, and he attacked Morgannwg several times. The Annales Cambriae (text A) were apparently compiled at his initiative.

personas/maredudd-ab-owain/resumen.texto: Second son of Owain ap Hywel Dda. Around 986 he took Gwynedd from Cadwallon ab Ieuaf, and when his father died, around 988, he also inherited Deheubarth, so that he could control almost all of Wales except Gwent and Morgannwg. According to the Welsh chronicles, in 987 Godfrey Haroldson raided Anglesey and carried off captives, and Maredudd paid a ransom (one silver coin per head, according to tradition); Viking raids were constant during his reign. At his death Gwynedd returned to the line of Idwal Foel with Cynan ap Hywel, and Deheubarth passed to a man called Rhain, whom the people of Deheubarth accepted as a son of Maredudd and whom the Welsh chronicles, after his defeat by Llywelyn ap Seisyll (1022), call an Irish pretender.

personas/maredudd-ab-owain-ab-edwin/resu.texto: Male-line descendant of Hywel Dda, he recovered Deheubarth in 1063, on the death of Gruffudd ap Llywelyn, who had taken it from his family, claiming rights through his mother Angharad. The Normans devastated south-eastern Wales during his reign; after some attempts, he did not resist their advance into Gwent and received lands in England in 1070. He died in 1072 in a battle by the River Rhymni, and was succeeded by his brother Rhys, not by his son Gruffudd.

hechos/crannogs/titulo.texto: Crannogs: Artificial Islands of Scotland and Ireland

hechos/crannogs/resumen.texto: Crannogs are artificial islets of wood, stone and earth built in lakes and estuaries, with one or more houses, used in Scotland and Ireland from the Late Bronze Age to the 17th century. The one at Oakbank, in Loch Tay, was dated to around 500 BC and preserved wood, seeds and even butter; in Ireland most are from the Early Middle Ages, and some, such as Lagore, were royal residences. It is debated whether they were mainly defensive or a way of showing rank.

hechos/cultura-de-arras/titulo.texto: The Arras Culture and Its Chariot Burials

hechos/cultura-de-arras/resumen.texto: In East Yorkshire, between the 4th and 1st centuries BC, the dead were buried under small barrows surrounded by square ditches, a custom rare in Britain and similar to that of Champagne. Some twenty graves held a two-wheeled chariot, as at Wetwang Slack (one of them a woman's, excavated in 2001) and Pocklington (2017, with its horses). Ptolemy places the Parisi there, namesakes of a Gaulish people, and since the 19th century it has been debated whether there was a migration from the continent; Ian Stead (1991) pointed out that the rites differ from continental ones in important details (the body in a crouched position, the dismantled chariot), and today contacts and small groups are thought more likely than an invasion.

hechos/escudo-de-battersea/resumen.texto: Bronze facing of a shield, decorated in La Tène style with curvilinear reliefs and red glass studs, found in the Thames in 1857 and now in the British Museum. It is too thin for combat, so it is considered a prestige object thrown into the river as an offering, like many other weapons from the Thames.

hechos/yelmo-de-waterloo/resumen.texto: Bronze-sheet helmet with two conical horns and La Tène decoration, found in the Thames beside Waterloo Bridge in 1868. According to the British Museum it is the only horned Iron Age helmet found in Europe; it was ceremonial, and the image of the Celtic (or Viking) warrior wearing horns as a norm has no archaeological support.

hechos/espejo-de-desborough/resumen.texto: Polished bronze mirror whose back is covered with a design of curves and spirals drawn with compasses, found in Northamptonshire in 1908. Decorated mirrors are a creation specific to Britain in the last century before the conquest, and several appear in women's graves.

hechos/tesoro-de-broighter/resumen.texto: Set of gold pieces found in 1896 near Limavady, in Ulster: a miniature boat with oars and mast, a bowl, chains and a large hollow torc decorated in La Tène style. The British Museum, which had bought it, argued that it was an offering to a sea god and not a hidden treasure; the court rejected this in 1903, the pieces passed to the Crown, and today they are in the National Museum of Ireland. It is one of the best examples of La Tène art in Ireland.

hechos/piedra-de-turoe/resumen.texto: Granite stone a little over one metre tall, its upper part covered with curvilinear La Tène reliefs, in County Galway. It is dated between the 1st century BC and the 1st century AD; its function is unknown, and it is compared with stones in Brittany and Germany, which feeds the discussion about how La Tène style reached Ireland.

hechos/calzada-de-corlea/resumen.texto: A kilometre-long track of oak planks laid over a bog in Longford, whose trees were felled, according to dendrochronology, in 148 BC. It was a work that required an authority capable of gathering a great deal of labor, and it sank into the bog a few years later; it has been linked to a causeway in the saga Tochmarc Étaíne.

hechos/gran-edificio-de-emain-macha/titu.texto: The Great Circular Building of Emain Macha

hechos/gran-edificio-de-emain-macha/resu.texto: On the summit of Emain Macha stood a circular structure about 40 metres in diameter, with an outer wall, four inner rings of posts and a large central oak post which, according to dendrochronology, was felled around 95 BC. Shortly afterward the interior was filled with stones, the timber was burned and everything was covered with earth, forming the present mound. Chris Lynn interprets it as a ritual act, perhaps to create access to the otherworld; it is unclear whether it had a roof or whether anyone lived there.

hechos/reyes-britanos-ante-augusto/titul.texto: British Kings Who Took Refuge with Augustus

hechos/reyes-britanos-ante-augusto/resum.texto: Augustus planned three times to invade Britain (Cassius Dio XLIX and LIII) and never did. Strabo (IV.5.3) explains that some British chiefs had won his friendship through embassies and offerings on the Capitol, and that the island yielded more in customs duties than it would as a province; in his Res Gestae (32) Augustus names two British kings who took refuge with him, Dubnovellaunus and Tincomarus.

hechos/invasiones-de-cesar-a-britania/re.texto: Caesar crossed to Britain in 55 BC with two legions and in 54 with five and some 800 ships, according to his Commentaries (BG IV.20-36 and V.1-23), which give as the reason the help the Britons gave the Gauls. In the first he barely left the coast of Kent; in the second he crossed the Thames, defeated Cassivellaunus, took hostages, set a tribute and protected the Trinovantes of Mandubracius, but returned to Gaul without leaving a garrison. Caesar wrote for the public of Rome, where the Senate voted twenty days of thanksgiving; historians see the expeditions as a prestige operation rather than a conquest, and the location of his landings is debated (in 2017 Pegwell Bay was proposed).

hechos/campana-de-caligula/resumen.texto: According to Suetonius (Caligula 44-47), Caligula led an army to the coast facing Britain after receiving the surrender of Adminius, son of Cunobelinus; he ordered the soldiers to gather seashells as “spoils of the Ocean” and had a lighthouse built. Suetonius, hostile to the emperor, tells it as a farce; some historians think it was an invasion aborted by a mutiny.

hechos/conquista-romana-de-britania/resu.texto: In 43 Claudius sent Aulus Plautius with four legions and auxiliary troops, some 40,000 men according to modern estimates (the sources give no figure), on the pretext of restoring Verica; they probably landed at Richborough. Within four years the southeast was conquered; thirty years of war followed in Wales and the north, with the resistance of Caratacus, the revolt of Boudica and that of Venutius, until the campaigns of Agricola in Scotland. The sources are Roman (Cassius Dio, Tacitus, Suetonius) and inscriptions; archaeology shows both destruction and forts and the rapid adoption of Roman life by the southern elites, which some historians (Mattingly) read as colonization and others as integration.

hechos/batalla-del-medway/resumen.texto: According to Cassius Dio (LX.20), the Britons of Caratacus and Togodumnus awaited the Romans behind a river, identified with the Medway, and the battle lasted two days, which was unusual at the time; Celtic auxiliary troops swam across with their weapons, and the future emperor Vespasian crossed at another point. The Britons withdrew to the Thames, where Togodumnus died.

hechos/claudio-en-camuloduno/resumen.texto: Claudius arrived in Britain with reinforcements, which according to Cassius Dio (LX.21) included elephants, crossed the Thames, took Camulodunum and received the surrender of several tribes; according to Suetonius (Claudius 17) he was on the island only sixteen days. He celebrated a triumph in 44, named his son Britannicus, and his arch in Rome proclaimed that he had received the surrender of eleven kings of Britain “without any loss.”

hechos/campana-de-vespasiano/resumen.texto: According to Suetonius (Vespasian 4), the future emperor, commanding Legion II Augusta, fought thirty battles, subdued two powerful peoples, took more than twenty oppida and the Isle of Wight. At Hod Hill Roman artillery projectiles appeared, along with a fort built inside the hillfort; at Maiden Castle, the “war cemetery” that Wheeler attributed to the Roman assault was later reinterpreted as a common cemetery with some victims of violence.

hechos/rebelion-de-los-icenos-de-47/resu.texto: Tacitus (Annals XII.31) tells that the governor Ostorius Scapula wanted to disarm the allied tribes south of the frontier, and that the Iceni, until then allies, rose up and were defeated in a fortified enclosure. It was the first clash with the people of Boudica, thirteen years before her revolt.

hechos/captura-de-carataco/resumen.texto: According to Tacitus (Annals XII.33-36), Caratacus awaited Ostorius Scapula on a hill protected by a river and stone walls in the land of the Ordovices, and was defeated; the Romans captured his wife, his daughter and his brothers. He fled to the queen of the Brigantes, Cartimandua, who handed him over in chains. The site of the battle has not been identified, although Caer Caradoc and other hills have been proposed.

hechos/discurso-de-carataco-en-roma/resu.texto: Caratacus was displayed in Rome with his family before the people and the Praetorian Guard. Tacitus (Annals XII.37) has him tell Claudius that, had he been moderate in his fortune, he would have entered as a friend and not as a captive; that it is not surprising that someone defends his horses, weapons and riches; and that if the Romans want to rule over everyone, it does not follow that everyone must accept servitude. Claudius pardoned him. The speech is a composition by Tacitus, following the custom of ancient historians of putting into their characters' mouths what they “must” have said, and it serves both to honor the vanquished and to show the emperor's clemency; Cassius Dio attributes to him another phrase about Roman greed.

hechos/masacre-de-mona/titulo.texto: The Roman Attack on Mona and the Druids

hechos/masacre-de-mona/resumen.texto: Tacitus (Annals XIV.29-30) tells that Suetonius Paulinus crossed the Menai Strait with flat-bottomed boats and horsemen who waded across, and that on the shore warriors awaited them, along with women dressed in black carrying torches, like Furies, and druids who raised their hands and hurled curses. After a first moment of paralysis the soldiers attacked, burned the enemy “in their own fire” and cut down the sacred groves, where, according to Tacitus, altars were sprinkled with the blood of captives. Tacitus wrote half a century later, and the scene serves to show barbarian “superstition”; archaeology has not found the massacre or the groves, although the Llyn Cerrig Bach deposit proves offerings on the island. News of Boudica's revolt interrupted the campaign.

hechos/rebelion-de-boudica/resumen.texto: After the death of Prasutagus, Roman officials plundered the kingdom of the Iceni, flogged his widow Boudica and raped his daughters, according to Tacitus (Annals XIV.31); the Iceni and the Trinovantes, also resentful of the confiscations for the colony of Camulodunum and of the loans demanded (Dio LXII.2), rose up while the governor was on Mona. They destroyed Camulodunum with its temple to Claudius, defeated Legion IX and razed Londinium and Verulamium, where, according to Tacitus, some 70,000 citizens and allies died (80,000 according to Dio); Suetonius Paulinus defeated them in a battle of unknown location, beside a Roman road, in which Tacitus gives 80,000 Britons dead against 400 Romans. The figures, which Tacitus takes from tradition and Dio inflates with an army of 230,000 rebels, are rhetorical and cannot be verified (Henige); archaeology confirms the destruction of the three cities.

hechos/capa-de-incendio-de-boudica/titul.texto: Boudica's Burn Layer at Colchester, London and St Albans

hechos/capa-de-incendio-de-boudica/resum.texto: Excavations at Colchester and London find everywhere a layer of burnt debris and reddened clay dated to around 60-61, which is identified with the destruction by Boudica; at Colchester, in 2014, a small hoard of jewelry hidden during the attack came to light under the floor of a house. At Verulamium the layer is more limited, and it is debated whether the city burned entirely. Almost no human remains associated with it have been found, which does not contradict the sources but makes it impossible to verify their death tolls.

hechos/rebelion-de-venucio/resumen.texto: According to Tacitus (Histories III.45), taking advantage of the Roman civil war of 69, Venutius, Queen Cartimandua's former husband, gathered the Brigantes opposed to her and to Rome and attacked her; the Romans could only rescue the queen, and “the kingdom went to Venutius, the war to us.” The campaigns of Petillius Cerialis between 71 and 74 ended Brigantian resistance.

hechos/campanas-de-agricola/resumen.texto: According to Tacitus, his father-in-law Agricola conquered the Ordovices and Mona, advanced through northern England and southern Scotland, built forts up to the Tay and in 83 or 84 defeated the Caledonians at Mons Graupius; his fleet sailed around Britain and confirmed that it was an island. Tacitus (Agricola 24) says that Agricola believed Ireland could be taken with a single legion and some auxiliaries, and that he had with him an exiled Irish king. Soon afterward Rome abandoned northern Scotland, including the legionary fortress of Inchtuthil, unfinished.

hechos/batalla-del-monte-graupio/resumen.texto: Battle in which Agricola defeated a coalition of Caledonians, according to Tacitus (Agricola 29-38) more than 30,000 men led by Calgacus, whose speech against Rome Tacitus composes. Tacitus gives 10,000 Caledonian dead against 360 Romans and says that the victory was won by the auxiliary troops, without the legions being used. The site has not been identified (Bennachie and other sites in northeast Scotland have been proposed), and the figures form part of the eulogy of his father-in-law.

hechos/muro-de-adriano/resumen.texto: Stone and turf wall of about 117 kilometres, from the Tyne to the Solway, which Hadrian ordered built from 122, according to the Historia Augusta, “to separate the barbarians from the Romans.” It had forts, a fortlet every mile, and a ditch to the south (the vallum), and it controlled passage and trade more than it prevented attacks; it was the frontier of the province for almost three centuries, except for the years of the Antonine Wall.

hechos/muro-de-antonino/resumen.texto: Turf wall of about 60 kilometres between the Forth and the Clyde, which Antoninus Pius ordered built from 142, according to the Historia Augusta, after a campaign of Lollius Urbicus in southern Scotland. It was abandoned around 160 and the army returned to Hadrian's Wall; its “distance slabs,” with reliefs of legionaries defeating Britons, are among the best sources on how Rome represented that war.

hechos/campanas-de-severo-en-caledonia/r.texto: Septimius Severus led a large army against the Caledonians and the Maeatae, who had broken their agreements with Rome. Cassius Dio (LXXVI.12-15 in Boissevain's numbering; LXXVII in the Loeb edition) describes them as having no cities or fields, living by hunting and herding, naked and with wives in common, and says that Rome lost 50,000 men; Herodian (III.14) adds that they tattooed their bodies with animal figures. Both repeat commonplaces about barbarians at the edge of the world. Severus died in York in 211 and his son Caracalla made peace.

hechos/primera-mencion-de-los-pictos/tit.texto: The First Mention of the Picts

hechos/primera-mencion-de-los-pictos/res.texto: A Latin panegyric addressed to Caesar Constantius Chlorus in 297 (Latin Panegyrics VIII.11) says that in Caesar's time the Britons knew only the Picts and the Hibernians as enemies, “still half-naked”: it is the first appearance of the name, which in Latin means “painted” and may have been a nickname given by Roman soldiers. The phrase “the forests and marshes of the Caledonians and other Picts” comes from another panegyric, addressed to Constantine in 310 (VI.7). From then on Roman sources call the peoples north of the wall Picts.

hechos/conspiracion-barbara/resumen.texto: Ammianus Marcellinus (XXVII.8) tells that in 367 Picts, Irish Scots and Attacotti attacked Britain at the same time as Franks and Saxons attacked Gaul, that they killed the count of the shore and that the Duke of Britain fell into an ambush. Count Theodosius, father of the emperor of the same name, restored control in 368; the idea of a coordinated attack belongs to the historian and is debated.

hechos/fin-de-la-britania-romana/resumen.texto: From 383, when Magnus Maximus took troops from Britain to contest the Empire, the island's garrison was gradually reduced. In 407 the army of Britain proclaimed Constantine III emperor, who crossed to Gaul with the island's troops. According to Zosimus (VI.5), in 409 the Britons expelled the Roman officials and defended themselves alone, and in 410 the emperor Honorius wrote to them that they should take care of their own defense (VI.10), although some historians think that letter was addressed to Bruttium, in Italy. Archaeology shows the end of coinage and of mass production around 400-430 and the gradual abandonment of towns and villas.

hechos/visita-de-german-de-auxerre/titul.texto: Germanus of Auxerre in Britain and the “Alleluia Victory”

hechos/visita-de-german-de-auxerre/resum.texto: According to Prosper of Aquitaine, in 429 Pope Celestine sent Germanus of Auxerre to Britain to fight the followers of Pelagius. Constantius of Lyon, who wrote around 480, tells that Germanus debated them before a crowd, visited the tomb of St Alban and led a British army to a victory without combat against Picts and Saxons, shouting “Alleluia.” It shows a Britain with bishops, romanized elites and external threats, seen from Gaul and through a hagiographer.

hechos/gemidos-de-los-britanos/resumen.texto: Gildas (De excidio 20) quotes a letter from the Britons to Agitius, “thrice consul,” usually identified with the general Aetius (consul for the third time in 446), with the phrase “the barbarians drive us to the sea, the sea drives us back to the barbarians.” It is the last known request for help from Rome, and it did not arrive; the date and context depend on the identification of Agitius and on Gildas's chronology, which is debated.

hechos/llegada-de-los-sajones/resumen.texto: Gildas tells that a “proud tyrant” and his council invited Saxons as mercenaries against the Picts and the Scots, and that these rebelled and devastated the island; Bede dates the arrival to around 449 and gives the names of Vortigern, Hengist and Horsa. The Gallic Chronicle of 452 says that in 441 Britain passed under the power of the Saxons. Archaeology and genetics show a significant migration from northern Germany and Denmark in the 5th and 6th centuries, more gradual and mixed with the British population than the account of a violent conquest suggests; its proportion and pace are debated (Halsall).

hechos/derrota-de-riotamo/titulo.texto: The Defeat of Riothamus at Déols

hechos/derrota-de-riotamo/resumen.texto: According to Jordanes (Getica 237-238), the emperor Anthemius asked the Britons for help against the Visigoths of Euric, and their king Riothamus arrived by sea with 12,000 men as far as the territory of the Bituriges; Euric defeated him at Déols before the Romans arrived, and Riothamus fled to the Burgundians. It is the largest documented British military action in Gaul.

hechos/emigracion-britona-a-armorica/res.texto: Between the 4th and 6th centuries many Britons from southwestern Britain and Wales settled in Armorica, which from then on was called Brittany; Gildas speaks of those who went “across the sea” singing psalms, and in 461 a “bishop of the Britons,” Mansuetus, signed at the council of Tours. Their monks, such as Samson of Dol, founded monasteries and bishoprics, and their language gave rise to Breton. Jackson (1953) saw in Breton a transplanted Brittonic; Fleuriot argued that it mixed with a Gaulish language still alive in Armorica, an idea most consider possible but unproven. The causes of the emigration (Saxon pressure, Irish raids, organized colonization) are debated.

hechos/obispado-de-britonia/titulo.texto: The Britons of Galicia and the Bishopric of Britonia

hechos/obispado-de-britonia/resumen.texto: A group of Britons settled in northern Galicia and Asturias in the 6th century; at the second council of Braga, in 572, Mailoc signed as bishop of the “Britonian church,” and the Suevic Parrochiale mentions its see. The bishopric, probably centered near Bretoña (Lugo), was lost in the 9th century to that of Mondoñedo; it is one of the few documented traces of that emigration in Hispania.

hechos/asentamientos-irlandeses-en-gales.texto: Irish Settlements in Wales and Cornwall

Between the 4th and 6th centuries Irish groups settled in southwestern Wales, northwestern Wales and Cornwall: this is shown by stones with inscriptions in ogham and Latin, which in Dyfed bear Irish names, and by Irish genealogical accounts such as The Expulsion of the Déisi. The Historia Brittonum attributes their expulsion from northern Wales to the sons of Cunedda, an account considered legendary.

hechos/batalla-de-badon/resumen.texto: Gildas (De excidio 26) mentions the siege of Mount Badon as the last great British victory over the Saxons, which gave them decades of peace, and says it happened in the year he was born, without naming the leader. The Historia Brittonum, three centuries later, lists it as the twelfth battle of Arthur, in which he supposedly killed 960 men alone, and the Annales Cambriae date it to 516. The probable date runs from 490 to 520, and the location is unknown (Bath, the Wiltshire hills and others have been proposed).

hechos/mision-de-paladio/titulo.texto: Palladius's Mission, First Bishop of Ireland

hechos/mision-de-paladio/resumen.texto: Prosper of Aquitaine records in his chronicle for 431 that Pope Celestine ordained Palladius and sent him as the first bishop “to the Scots who believe in Christ.” It is the oldest and firmest date for Irish Christianity, and it proves that Christian communities already existed, probably through contact with Britain; tradition overshadowed it with the figure of Patrick.

hechos/mision-de-patricio/resumen.texto: Patrick, a Briton captured as a youth by Irish pirates, returned as a bishop and missionary in the 5th century; in his Confessio he tells of baptisms, ordinations, gifts to kings and dangers, without giving dates or places. His traditional date of arrival, 432, was fixed centuries later so that it would follow that of Palladius, and the annals record his death in 457 or 461 and also in 492 or 493: hence two chronologies, an “early” one (432-461) and a “late” one (around 460-493), which many specialists in early medieval Ireland prefer. T. F. O'Rahilly (1942) proposed that tradition merged two people into one Patrick, one of them Palladius. His activity is located mainly in the north of the island. The accounts of his confrontation with King Loegaire and the druids at Tara are from Muirchú and Tírechán, two centuries later, and serve the claims of Armagh.

hechos/ultima-feis-de-tara/resumen.texto: The Annals of Ulster record in 560 the “feast of Tara” (feis Temro) of Diarmait mac Cerbaill, the last one mentioned. The feis is interpreted as a royal inauguration rite with pre-Christian roots, a “marriage” of the king with sovereignty, and its disappearance as an effect of Christianization; the information is scarce and the interpretation rests on later literary texts.

hechos/batalla-de-cul-dreimne/resumen.texto: Battle near Ben Bulben, in Sligo, in which the northern Uí Néill, kinsmen of Columba, defeated Diarmait mac Cerbaill, king of Tara. Adomnán mentions the battle and an excommunication of Columba; later legend explains it by a psalter copy that Columba made in secret (the Cathach) and says the saint left Ireland as a penance, a version historians consider late.

hechos/fundacion-de-iona/titulo.texto: Columba Founds the Monastery of Iona

hechos/fundacion-de-iona/resumen.texto: In 563, according to the Annals of Ulster and Adomnán, Columba left Ireland with twelve companions and founded a monastery on the island of Iona, granted by the king of Dál Riata or by the Picts, depending on the source. Iona became the head of a network of monasteries in Ireland and Scotland, the center from which the Picts and the Northumbrian Angles were converted, and probably the place where the Book of Kells was begun.

hechos/visita-de-columba-a-bridei/titulo.texto: Columba Visits the Pictish King Bridei

hechos/visita-de-columba-a-bridei/resume.texto: Adomnán (II.33-35) tells that Columba traveled to the fortress of King Bridei near the River Ness, that he miraculously opened its gates, and that he confronted the king's magician, Broichan. Bede (III.4) says that Columba converted the northern Picts; historians see a slower conversion, in which the visit was mainly diplomatic.

hechos/sinodo-de-birr/titulo.texto: The Synod of Birr and Adomnán's Law

hechos/sinodo-de-birr/resumen.texto: In 697, at an assembly in Birr, Abbot Adomnán of Iona promulgated the Cáin Adomnáin, “law of the innocents,” which protected women, children and clerics from violence in war, with fines for anyone who violated it. It was guaranteed by 91 notables, laymen and churchmen, from Ireland, Dál Riata and the Pictish kingdom, whose list survives; it is one of the earliest laws protecting non-combatants in Europe.

hechos/asentamiento-de-dal-riata/titulo.texto: The Gaelic Kingdom of Dál Riata

hechos/asentamiento-de-dal-riata/resumen.texto: Gaelic kingdom that covered northern Antrim in Ireland and Argyll and the western islands of Scotland, centered on Dunadd. Medieval tradition has it founded by Fergus Mór, who supposedly crossed from Ireland around 500, and Bede speaks of Scots who came with their chief Reuda. Ewan Campbell (2001) argued that archaeology shows no migration and that Gaelic may have been spoken in Argyll long before; other historians maintain that there was an expansion from Ireland, though smaller and earlier than the traditional account.

hechos/batalla-de-catraeth/resumen.texto: Battle known only from the Gododdin, in which a band of warriors gathered by Mynyddog Mwynfawr at Din Eidyn (Edinburgh) died almost entirely while attacking the Angles of Deira and Bernicia at Catraeth, usually identified with Catterick. The poem mourns them and praises each warrior; the date, around 600, and even the historical character of the episode depend on the dating of the poem, which is debated.

hechos/batalla-de-degsastan/resumen.texto: According to Bede (I.34), Áedán mac Gabráin, king of Dál Riata, attacked the English king Æthelfrith of Bernicia with a large army and was defeated with heavy losses, and “from then on no king of the Scots dared to make war on the English.” The location has not been identified.

hechos/batalla-de-chester/resumen.texto: King Æthelfrith of Northumbria defeated the Britons of Powys near Chester, between 613 and 616. Bede (II.2) tells that before the battle he had some 1200 monks of the monastery of Bangor-is-y-coed, who were praying for the Britons, put to death, and presents it as divine punishment because the Britons did not accept the authority of Augustine of Canterbury. The figure comes from an author hostile to the Britons and cannot be verified.

hechos/batalla-de-hatfield-chase/resumen.texto: Cadwallon, British king of Gwynedd, and Penda, pagan king of Mercia, defeated and killed Edwin, the first Christian king of Northumbria, on 12 October 633. Bede (II.20) tells that Cadwallon laid waste Northumbria “with barbarous cruelty,” sparing neither women nor children; the following year Oswald defeated him and killed him. It was the last great British offensive against the English kingdoms.

hechos/batalla-de-dun-nechtain/resumen.texto: On 20 May 685 the Pictish king Bridei mac Bili defeated and killed Ecgfrith of Northumbria, who had entered Pictish territory. Bede (IV.26) tells that from then on the Picts, the Scots and part of the Britons regained their freedom. It was traditionally placed at Dunnichen, in Angus, and a stone at Aberlemno with a battle scene has been associated with it; Alex Woolf (2006) proposed Dunachton, in Badenoch, further north.

hechos/expulsion-del-clero-de-iona/titul.texto: King Nechtan Expels the Clergy of Iona

hechos/expulsion-del-clero-de-iona/resum.texto: The Annals of Ulster record in 717 “the expulsion of the community of Iona beyond the spine of Britain by King Nechtan.” It followed the adoption by the Pictish king of the Roman Easter and tonsure, which Bede (V.21) describes in detail, and it cut the Pictish Church off from the influence of Iona.

hechos/conquista-de-dal-riata-por-oengus.texto: Óengus of the Picts Subdues Dál Riata

The Annals of Ulster record that in 736 the Pictish king Óengus mac Fergusa devastated Dál Riata, took Dunadd and chained two sons of King Selbach, and that in 741 there was “the defeat of Dál Riata by Óengus.” For some decades Dál Riata was under Pictish rule, a century before the union of Picts and Scots under a Gaelic dynasty.

hechos/ataques-vikingos-a-iona/resumen.texto: The Annals of Ulster record raids by the “gentiles” against Iona in 795, 802 and 806, when sixty-eight members of the community were killed. The monks moved to Kells, where they built a new monastery from 807; Iona remained a place of pilgrimage and of royal burial.

hechos/union-de-pictos-y-escotos/titulo.texto: The Union of Picts and Scots and the Kingdom of Alba

hechos/union-de-pictos-y-escotos/resumen.texto: Scottish chronicles from the 10th to the 12th centuries tell that Cináed mac Ailpín, king of the Scots of Dál Riata, conquered the Picts around 843, and tradition made him the first king of Scotland. The Annals of Ulster call him “king of the Picts” in 858, and the title “king of Alba” first appears with Domnall II in 900. Present-day historians (Woolf, Broun) see a gradual process in which the Pictish defeat by the Vikings in 839 and the Gaelicization of the elite made the Pictish language and identity disappear, without the conquest or extermination told in the legends.

hechos/asedio-de-alt-clut/titulo.texto: The Viking siege of Alt Clut

hechos/asedio-de-alt-clut/resumen.texto: The Annals of Ulster record that in 870 the Viking kings of Dublin, Amlaíb and Ímar, besieged the rock of Alt Clut for four months and in the end took it and sacked it; the following year they returned to Dublin with many captives, Britons, Angles and Picts. The British kingdom continued centred on Govan under the name Strathclyde.

hechos/batalla-de-brunanburh/resumen.texto: In 937 the English king Athelstan defeated a coalition of Olaf Guthfrithson, Norse king of Dublin, Constantine II, king of Alba, and Owain, British king of Strathclyde. It is celebrated in an Old English poem in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and recorded in the Annals of Ulster as a “great, lamentable and horrible” battle, and in the Annales Cambriae. The location has been much debated and is usually placed today at Bromborough, on the Wirral peninsula. The Welsh kings, subject to Athelstan, did not take part, and the Armes Prydein is usually read as the voice of those who wanted such an alliance.

hechos/dique-de-offa/resumen.texto: An earthwork with a ditch some 130 kilometres long between Mercia and the Welsh kingdoms, which Asser attributes to King Offa of Mercia (757–796) at the end of the 9th century, “from sea to sea”. It was the symbolic border between English and Welsh; radiocarbon dating in recent years suggests that some stretches predate Offa.

hechos/tratado-de-montgomery/resumen.texto: Treaty by which King Henry III of England recognized Llywelyn ap Gruffudd as Prince of Wales and lord of the other Welsh nobles, in exchange for homage and 25,000 marks. It was the high point of the independent Welsh principality.

hechos/muerte-de-llywelyn-en-cilmeri/tit.texto: The death of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd at Cilmeri

hechos/muerte-de-llywelyn-en-cilmeri/res.texto: On 11 December 1282 Llywelyn ap Gruffudd died near Cilmeri, separated from his army, in a clash with English troops whose details vary according to the chronicle; his head was displayed in London. The elegy by Gruffudd ab yr Ynad Coch mourned him as the end of the world, and tradition calls him “the last leader” of Wales.

hechos/conquista-eduardiana-de-gales/tit.texto: The conquest of Wales by Edward I

hechos/conquista-eduardiana-de-gales/res.texto: Edward I defeated Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in 1277 and reduced him to Gwynedd with the Treaty of Aberconwy; after the uprising of 1282 he conquered the principality, executed Dafydd ap Gruffudd in 1283 and annexed it with the Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284. The castles of Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech and Beaumaris secured the conquest; Welsh law remained in force in civil matters until the Acts of Union of 1535–1542.

hechos/conquista-de-mona-por-agricola/re.texto: Mona (Anglesey), the center of the druids, had been attacked in 61 by Suetonius Paulinus (Annals XIV.29), who had to withdraw because of Boudica’s revolt. Tacitus, who wrote as Agricola’s son-in-law and is the only written source for the second invasion, recounts that in the autumn of 77 Agricola, after exterminating, according to Tacitus, almost the entire Ordovices people of northern Wales (“caesa prope universa gente”), had hand-picked auxiliaries cross the strait without boats, and the islanders, who were expecting a fleet, surrendered (Agricola 18). The island remained under Roman rule until the 5th century; archaeology has found a fort near Cemlyn Bay and a village, but no villa or major civic center.

hechos/costa-sajona/resumen.texto: Late Roman military command and a chain of forts on both sides of the Channel, under the “Count of the Saxon Shore,” established at the end of the 3rd century. In Britain, forts with very high walls survive in eastern and southeastern England (Brancaster, Caister and Reculver from the 230s; the rest between 270 and 290). Only the Notitia Dignitatum, from the late 4th century, uses the name, and it is debated what “Saxon” means (a coast attacked by Saxons or settled by them) and what the forts were for: defense against Germanic pirates, according to the traditional reading. John Cotterill judges the threat exaggerated, and D. A. White proposed that they were raised during the secession of Carausius and Allectus (289–296).

hechos/gask-ridge/lugar.texto: Gask Ridge (near Strageath fort, reference point)

hechos/gask-ridge/resumen.texto: Series of Flavian-era Roman forts, fortlets and watchtowers along about 16 km of ridge north of the River Earn, in Perthshire, near the edge of the Highlands. It was built around 70–80 and was in use for only a few years, probably fewer than ten; Hadrian’s Wall was begun some 42 years later. It may be the oldest fortified land frontier of Rome. Its function is debated: to contain raids from the Highlands (although only the legionary fortress at Inchtuthil had the strength to do so), or to guard the route to the estuary ports of the Tay and the Forth.

hechos/batalla-de-deorham/resumen.texto: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, under the year 577, says that Ceawlin and Cuthwine of Wessex defeated the Britons, killed three kings (Coinmail, Condidan and Farinmail) and took Gloucester, Cirencester and Bath; this is the only evidence. Historians of the 19th century and much of the 20th (Guest, Stenton, Myres) saw it as the break that left the Britons isolated in Wales and Cornwall. Today the date and the importance of those cities are doubted, and the account may reflect the kingdoms of the 9th and 10th centuries in which the Chronicle was compiled (Collins, Yorke, Halsall), although not all deny that it happened.

hechos/campana-de-constancio-contra-los-.texto: Campaign of Constantius I against the Picts

In 305 Constantius I, by then Augustus, crossed to Britain, travelled to the north of the island and launched an expedition against the Picts; c. 7 January 306 he assumed the title Britannicus Maximus II. He spent the winter in Eboracum (York) and died there on 25 July 306, without having continued the campaign; the troops proclaimed his son Constantine emperor.

hechos/batalla-de-tara-980/resumen.texto: In 980 Máel Sechnaill mac Domnaill, king of Mide, defeated near the Hill of Tara the Norse of Dublin, led by Ragnall, son of King Amlaíb Cuarán, with troops from the islands; Ragnall died and Amlaíb withdrew to Iona. The Annals of Ulster (U980.1) record the battle, the slaughter and the death of Ragnall. According to the Annals of the Four Masters (M979.6, compiled in 1632–1636) and the Annals of Tigernach (T980.4), Máel Sechnaill and the king of Ulaid besieged Dublin for three days and three nights, took hostages and freed the Uí Néill from tribute, and Máel Sechnaill proclaimed that the captive Gaels should return to their land.

lugares/maiden-castle/resumen.texto: One of the largest hillforts in Europe, in Dorset, built around 600 BC over a Neolithic enclosure and enlarged with several lines of ramparts and ditches. Mortimer Wheeler excavated it in 1934–1937 and interpreted a group of burials, one with a Roman arrowhead lodged in a vertebra, as the “war cemetery” of Vespasian’s assault in 43–44; the excavations of Niall Sharples (1985–1986) showed that it was a cemetery used for a time and that there is no evidence of a great siege.

lugares/danebury/resumen.texto: Hillfort in Hampshire excavated over twenty years (1969–1988) by Barry Cunliffe, the most studied in Britain. Its hundreds of storage pits and raised granaries and its round houses led Cunliffe to see it as a “central place” that stored and redistributed the production of the region; J. D. Hill and others disputed that model and read ritual deposits in the pits.

lugares/hengistbury-head/resumen.texto: Headland on the Dorset coast that in the 1st century BC was Britain’s main port in trade with Armorica: Cunliffe found there amphorae of Italic wine (Dressel 1A), Armorican coins and metalworking debris. It shows exchange with Gaul before Caesar’s expeditions, which, in his view, was cut off after the war against the Veneti.

lugares/camuloduno/resumen.texto: Oppidum of the Trinovantes and later capital of Cunobelinus, surrounded by huge ramparts, where Claudius entered in 43. Rome founded there in 49 the first veterans’ colony in Britain, with a temple to the emperor Claudius, and Boudica razed it in 60 or 61; a layer of burnt red earth marks that destruction across the whole town.

lugares/verulamio/resumen.texto: Oppidum of the Catuvellauni, where Tasciovanus minted coins, and later a Roman municipium, which Tacitus counts among the cities destroyed by Boudica. It was one of the largest cities of Roman Britain; there Saint Alban, the first martyr of Britain, was venerated, and his tomb was visited by Germanus of Auxerre in 429.

lugares/stanwick/resumen.texto: Huge earthwork enclosure of more than 300 hectares in North Yorkshire, centre of the Brigantes. Wheeler interpreted it in 1951 as the last stronghold of Venutius against Rome; excavations by Colin Haselgrove showed a high-status site with tableware, glass and even Roman roof tiles from the 40s to the 70s AD, which is better associated with the court of Cartimandua, Rome’s ally.

lugares/fishbourne/resumen.texto: Large residence in Italic style near Chichester, with mosaics and gardens, the largest Roman building of its type north of the Alps. It was built around 75–80 over military installations from the conquest and is usually attributed to the client king Togidubnus, although no inscription confirms it; it burned around 270.

lugares/calleva/resumen.texto: Oppidum of the Atrebates, named on the coins of Epillus (CALLEV), and later a Roman town with walls, forum and amphitheatre. Abandoned between the 5th and 7th centuries, it was never resettled, which allowed it to be excavated almost entirely; one of the oldest churches known in Britain was found there.

lugares/snettisham/resumen.texto: Norfolk site in the land of the Iceni, where between 1948 and 1992 several hoards appeared containing more than 150 torcs or torc fragments of gold, silver and alloys, more than 70 of them complete, buried around 70 BC (the date is given by Gaulish coins found with them). It is the largest Iron Age treasure in Britain; among the pieces is the Great Torc of Snettisham, now in the British Museum. Whether they were offerings or a stored treasure is debated.

lugares/lago-de-glastonbury/resumen.texto: Iron Age village built on an artificial platform in the Somerset marshes, excavated by Arthur Bulleid between 1892 and 1907. The wood, textiles and objects preserved by the water make it a reference for everyday life in the period.

lugares/south-cadbury/resumen.texto: Hillfort in Somerset occupied since the Neolithic, fortified in the Iron Age and taken by the Romans. Leslie Alcock excavated it in 1966–1970 and found that around 470–500 someone rebuilt its ramparts and erected a great hall, with pottery imported from the Mediterranean; the identification with the Camelot of Arthur, proposed by John Leland in the 16th century, has no basis in the sources.

lugares/vindolanda/resumen.texto: Roman fort south of Hadrian’s Wall, earlier than the wall, where from 1973 onwards hundreds of wooden tablets inscribed in ink, dating to around 90–120, came to light. They were the oldest handwritten documents in Britain until the Bloomberg tablets from London, dating from 57 onwards, appeared.

lugares/anglesey/resumen.texto: Island in north-west Wales, the Roman Mona, which Tacitus describes as a refuge for fugitives and a centre of the druids. Suetonius Paulinus attacked it in 60 and Agricola conquered it in 77 or 78; at Llyn Cerrig Bach a large Iron Age deposit of weapons and objects was found. In the Middle Ages it was the centre of the kingdom of Gwynedd.

lugares/traprain-law/resumen.texto: East Lothian hill with a large fortified enclosure, probably the centre of the Votadini, the people whom the Welsh texts call Gododdin. In 1919 a hoard of more than twenty kilos of Roman silver cut into pieces appeared there, buried around 400–450, which shows the payments or gifts of Rome to peoples beyond the wall.

lugares/broch-de-mousa/resumen.texto: The best-preserved broch, a circular dry-stone tower with double walls and some 13 metres high on an island in Shetland, probably built in the last centuries BC. Norse sagas mention it as a refuge around 900 and in 1153. Brochs, some five hundred in northern and western Scotland, are debated as fortresses, houses of important lineages or symbols of prestige.

lugares/broch-de-gurness/resumen.texto: Orkney broch surrounded by a small village of stone houses, with walls and ditches for defence, from the Iron Age. Later the Picts occupied it, and afterwards there was a Viking grave there.

lugares/burghead/resumen.texto: Moray promontory with the largest known Pictish fort, with stone and timber ramparts, occupied between the 4th and 10th centuries and probably burnt by the Vikings. Stone plaques with carved bulls and a well cut into the rock were found there.

lugares/dunadd/resumen.texto: Hillfort in Argyll, centre of the Gaelic kingdom of Dál Riata. On the rock at the summit are carved a footprint, a basin, a boar and an Ogham inscription, usually associated with the inauguration of kings; the Annals of Ulster record that it was besieged in 683 and taken by the Pictish king Óengus in 736. Pottery and glass imported from the continent were found there.

lugares/whithorn/resumen.texto: Galloway site where, according to Bede, Bishop Ninian built a stone church, Candida Casa. The stone of Latinus, from around 450, is the oldest Christian monument in Scotland, and excavations show a settlement with Mediterranean imports and later an Anglian monastery and bishopric.

lugares/alt-clut/resumen.texto: Volcanic rock above the Clyde, stronghold of the British kings of Alt Clut, the kingdom later called Strathclyde; Adomnán names its king Rhydderch. The Vikings of Dublin took it in 870 after four months of siege.

lugares/tintagel/resumen.texto: Promontory on the Cornish coast where, in the 5th and 6th centuries, there was a high-status settlement with abundant pottery imported from the eastern Mediterranean and Hispania, probably a centre of the kings of Dumnonia. Geoffrey of Monmouth placed the conception of Arthur there, and the present castle was built by Richard of Cornwall in the 13th century; in 1998 the Artognou stone appeared.

lugares/dinas-emrys/resumen.texto: Hillfort in Snowdonia where the Historia Brittonum places the story of Vortigern, the tower that kept collapsing and the red and white dragons that the boy Ambrosius (Emrys) reveals. Excavations found occupation from the 5th and 6th centuries, with imported pottery.

lugares/st-davids/resumen.texto: Monastery founded, according to tradition, by David in the far west of Wales, the most important episcopal see in the country. It was sacked repeatedly by the Vikings; its present cathedral dates from the 12th century.

lugares/aberffraw/resumen.texto: Village in Anglesey that was the main seat of the kings and princes of Gwynedd; from the 12th century the Llywelyns styled themselves “princes of Aberffraw and lords of Snowdon”. Their court disappeared after the English conquest of 1282.

lugares/colina-de-tara/resumen.texto: Hill in Meath with monuments from a Neolithic passage tomb (the “mound of the hostages”, around 3000 BC) to Iron Age enclosures such as Ráith na Ríg. Medieval literature made it the seat of the high king of Ireland, a title claimed by the Uí Néill; surveys by the Discovery Programme show a large ceremonial complex, not a town or a palace.

lugares/emain-macha/resumen.texto: Ceremonial enclosure near Armagh, capital of the kings of Ulster in the sagas of the Ulster cycle. The excavations of Dudley Waterman (1961–1971) found a huge circular timber building some 40 metres across, with a central post felled, according to dendrochronology, around 95 BC; shortly afterwards it was filled with stones, burnt and covered with earth, a ritual act with no clear parallels. A skull of a Barbary macaque also appeared there, evidence of distant contacts.

lugares/dun-ailinne/resumen.texto: Ceremonial enclosure of some 13 hectares on a hill in Kildare, considered in the Middle Ages the site of the inauguration of the kings of Leinster. The excavations of Bernard Wailes (1968–1975) found a succession of large Iron Age circular timber structures, similar to those of Emain Macha, and animal bones from feasts, but very few traces of everyday life.

lugares/rathcroghan/resumen.texto: Complex of more than two hundred monuments in Roscommon, the Cruachan of the sagas, seat of the kings of Connacht and of Queen Medb in the Táin. The cave of Oweynagat, which the literature presents as an entrance to the otherworld, has a lintel with an Ogham inscription; geophysical surveys revealed large timber enclosures beneath the main mound.

lugares/uisneach/resumen.texto: Hill in Westmeath that medieval tradition considered the centre of Ireland and the site of a great assembly at Beltaine. It has monuments from the Neolithic and an enclosure from the Iron Age and the Early Middle Ages; the “stone of the divisions” would mark the point where the provinces met.

lugares/dun-aonghasa/resumen.texto: Stone fort on a cliff edge on Inishmore, in the Aran Islands, with a field of stakes (chevaux de frise) to slow attackers. Excavations by the Discovery Programme dated its first construction to around 1100 BC, in the Bronze Age, with alterations in the Iron Age and the Early Middle Ages.

lugares/grianan-de-aileach/resumen.texto: Circular stone fort on a hill in Donegal, seat of the northern Uí Néill, on a site occupied earlier. The annals record that the king of Munster, Muirchertach Ua Briain, destroyed it in 1101; what is seen today is largely a 19th-century reconstruction.

lugares/roca-de-cashel/resumen.texto: Rock in Tipperary, seat of the Eóganachta kings of Munster from the 5th century according to tradition, which linked it to a visit by Patrick. Brian Boru reigned from there, and in 1101 his great-grandson Muirchertach Ua Briain gave it to the Church; its present buildings date from the 12th to the 15th centuries.

lugares/kildare/resumen.texto: Double monastery of nuns and monks founded, according to tradition, by Brigid, which Cogitosus describes in the 7th century as the head of almost all the churches of Ireland, with a large timber church divided for men and women. Giraldus Cambrensis saw there in the 12th century the perpetual fire tended by nuns.

lugares/clonard/resumen.texto: Monastery in Meath founded by Finnian of Clonard, whom later tradition made the teacher of the “twelve apostles of Ireland”, among them Columba and Ciarán. It was a great centre of learning until it was sacked by the Vikings and by the Irish between the 9th and 12th centuries.

lugares/bangor-irlanda/resumen.texto: Ulster monastery founded by Comgall around 558, from which Columbanus left for the continent; the Antiphonary of Bangor, from the late 7th century, comes from there. The Vikings sacked it in 824.

lugares/glendalough/resumen.texto: Monastery founded by Kevin in a glacial valley in Wicklow, which grew into a pilgrimage centre with several churches and a round tower, which survive. It was sacked repeatedly in the 9th–11th centuries and fell within the diocese of Dublin in 1214.

lugares/skellig-michael/resumen.texto: Monastery on the summit of a rocky islet 12 kilometres off the coast of Kerry, with beehive-shaped stone cells: the extreme example of the asceticism of Irish monasticism. The annals record a Viking attack in 824; the monks left around the 13th century. It is a World Heritage Site.

lugares/monasterboice/resumen.texto: Louth monastery founded, according to tradition, by Buite at the end of the 5th century, famous for its tall 10th-century stone crosses, among them the Cross of Muiredach, with carved biblical scenes: one of the finest examples of early medieval Irish sculpture.
